get.description:
Everything an actor effectively holds, attributed to its source.

One entry per *(authority, pattern)* pair rather than a deduplicated set:
an actor commonly holds the same pattern through a role bundle **and** a
direct grant, and collapsing them would destroy the answer to "what actually
changes if I revoke this?".

``revocable_by_caller`` is resolved here because it depends on the caller,
not on the entry. It is computed with the same ``covers_any`` the service's
no-escalation check uses, so the control a UI offers and the refusal the
service would issue cannot disagree — but it is **advisory**: revocation
still goes through ``AuthzGrantService``, which re-runs the check.

schema.title: Response List Effective Permissions V1 Orgs  Org Id  Permissions Get

get.description:
What the **caller** may do in this org — so a UI can disable what it may not.

Answers every permission an org route enforces, from the same engine and
resolved actor the gates use (:func:`actor_permission_answers`), so the
control a UI greys out and the 403 the route would return cannot disagree.
Advisory only: every route still enforces its own gate.

Cost is one grant resolution for the caller plus an in-memory engine check
per enforced permission — caller-scoped, never a scan over other actors.

Gated on ``authz:permission.read`` like the rest of this router. Every org
role holds it, which is what lets a viewer learn it is a viewer; and a
caller reading its *own* authority learns nothing it could not discover by
trying the routes.

Everything that *can* be granted — not merely what somebody holds.

The other reads on this router describe a holder, so none of them can name a
permission nobody has yet, and a UI built on them can only ever render
authority that already exists. This is the endpoint that lets one show the
whole grantable set and mark which entries are enabled.

**Two sources, unioned**: the permissions the API's own route gates name, and
the requirements in ``tool_catalog_permissions``. Either alone omits real
permissions — the tool side cannot see the human-only surface
(``platform:*``, ``member:invitation.*``, ``authz:permission.*``), and the
route side cannot see a tool requirement no endpoint gates. Role bundles are
deliberately *not* a third source: they are pattern-valued, hold almost no
fully-concrete patterns, and a ``None`` axis cannot be expanded without the
very universe this endpoint builds. They serve instead as its completeness
oracle, asserted in the tests.

**Wildcards are entries, not something the caller expands.** Every wildcard
shape carries its own ``id``, so a held grant maps to exactly one entry
whatever its shape and ``audit:*.*`` ticks the domain-scope entry rather than
fanning out over the six audit leaves. That matters because expanding it
would report "6 of 6", when the grant actually covers every audit permission
*including ones that do not exist yet* — under-reporting reach, which is the
dangerous direction here. See ``covers_uncatalogued``.

The catalogue is platform vocabulary rather than org data, so the response
does not vary by ``org_id``; the route is org-scoped because it is called
from an org's permissions UI, and org-scoping is what keeps the
org-membership check and org MFA in the chain.

Read-only, and decides nothing: it never consults an actor, grant, or role
assignment.

**It lists what the platform *enforces*, which is narrower than what the
grant API will accept — so a consumer must render this catalogue UNION the
actor's held permissions, never the catalogue alone.**
``AuthzGrantService.grant`` checks only that the granter's own patterns
cover the requested one; it never consults this catalogue. An org owner
holding ``org:*.*`` can therefore write an inert but valid pattern such as
``org:fleet.merge``, which no route gates and no tool requires, and the
actor will hold a row with no entry here. Rendering the catalogue alone
would silently drop that grant — the very failure this endpoint exists to
fix, reintroduced one layer up. See ``is_exhaustive``.

Gated on the same ``authz:permission.read`` that gates reading who holds
what — the grantable vocabulary and the current assignments are the two
halves of one view, and splitting their gates would let a caller see one
without the other for no security benefit.

Who holds a permission — by direct grant, by role, and by self grant.

All three paths, because a lookup covering only some of them reports a
subset as though it were the whole set, and "no holders" reads as a finding
rather than as a gap.

Every holder carries its ``scope`` and its ``scope_shape``, and callers must
render the **three** shapes distinguishably: authority over every instance of
the kind, over one named record, or over everything belonging to one named
record. The same permission triple can name any of them, and merging them
reports the holder of a narrow grant as holding broad authority over every
instance.

Group by permission **and** shape, then name the members inside; never group
across shapes. ``anchored`` is part of the vocabulary from today even though
nothing emits it until anchored scope ships, so a client written against this
payload now needs no change when it starts appearing.

Takes a **concrete** permission, so all three axes are required: this
answers "who can do this specific thing" (``matches`` semantics). Wildcard
grants are still found — a ``secret:*`` row genuinely confers
``secret:secret.create`` and appears here.

schema.title: Response List Permission Holders V1 Orgs  Org Id  Permission Holders Get

get.description:
Which assigned tools would stop working if this grant were revoked.

Feeds the confirm step of a revoke. **Impact is a difference, not a pattern
match**: a tool counts only if it is assigned, works now, and would not work
after the removal. A tool still covered by another grant or by the role floor
is unaffected and is not counted — an over-reporting confirmation is worse
than none, because it teaches people to click through the dialog that exists
to stop them.

Read-only. Revoking still goes through ``AuthzGrantService``; this endpoint
cannot remove anything, and re-granting re-adds no tools because the grant
path never touches assignment.

Which tools a role-bundle change would disable, **across the whole org**.

The wide case, and the reason a preview exists at all. The bot-carried role
keys have no assignment table — every bot in the org holds them
unconditionally — so deleting one ``role_permissions`` row can strip tools
fleet-wide from a single click. ``bot_count`` and ``tool_count`` are served
so the warning can be specific (*"removes 37 tools across 9 bots"*) rather
than vague, and so the headline cannot disagree with the detail beneath it.

post.description:
Grant one permission pattern to one actor in this organization.

Holding ``authz:permission.create`` is necessary but **not sufficient**: the
service additionally refuses to grant any pattern the granter does not hold
itself (403), refuses to write into another organization (403), and refuses
``platform:team.manage`` to a non-human (403). Those refusals are raised by
the service and surfaced by the registered exception handlers — this route
does not re-check, re-word, or catch them.

delete.description:
Revoke a direct grant by id.

A grant id is a **global** handle, so the route's org prefix is not what
contains this: the service re-derives the row's own organization and applies
tenant containment plus authority over the pattern being removed. Without
that, any caller reaching this endpoint could strip authority from an actor
in another organization. Revocation removes authority rather than adding it,
so it cannot escalate — but it is emphatically not unauthenticated, and it is
audited with the same weight as a grant.

post.description:
Create bots, each with a pack installed: every one, or none.

Each bot takes the pack's name (unless `name` is given) and its avatar, and
starts on the pack's recommended model when one of the org's LLM credentials
can run it; otherwise it keeps the default model and `model` says why. The
pack is then installed exactly as `POST …/packs/installs` would, and what
the install could not bind by itself is reported in `setups`.

One transaction: if any bot or install is refused, no bot is created.
Needs `bot:bot.create` plus what installing a pack needs.

Create a new bot with the same definition as an existing one.

Copies what the source bot *is*: its config, managed workspace files,
skills, tools, tool domain settings, credential assignments, and
(by default) its Runtime Vault policy links. Does not copy what it has
*lived* — memory, conversations, disk, schedules, devices, health, its
email address, or its access list. The caller becomes the copy's owner.

Two gates apply. ``bot:bot.create`` because this creates a bot, and so the
copy is metered and capped exactly like any other creation
(``MeterKey.BOT_COUNT``); and bot ownership of the *source*, because
copying reads its whole definition — including which secrets it can reach.

patch.description:
Update bot metadata, compute overrides, or runtime privilege mode.

Tier, resource-override, and runtime privilege changes trigger a full K8s
reconcile. Avatar changes are metadata-only. For config changes, use PATCH
/{bot_slug}/config.

Per-bot resource overrides are available on every plan (bounded by the
plan's ``resource_maximums``). Privileged runtime mode is still gated to
plans with the ``privileged_mode`` feature; plans without it receive 403
``upgrade_required``.

delete.description: Set desired_state=deleted and enqueue reconcile notification.

get.description:
Lightweight readiness signals for chat surfaces (widget/console).

Cheap, pollable signal: ``llm_configured`` lets a surface warn — before any
send — that the bot can't respond until a credential is assigned, and
``maintenance_restart_pending`` drives a subtle "restart pending" indicator
while a workload-aware maintenance restart is in flight. Visibility-gated
exactly like ``get_bot`` so restricted bots stay 404-invisible to actors
without access.
Get live runtime storage, memory, and CPU usage for a bot.

post.description:
Restart a bot runtime container.

Normally this mirrors the operator/k9s recovery action: the provisioner
deletes the current pod and the deployment recreates it. Visibility alone is
not enough for this mutating runtime action — org owners/platform admins may
restart any visible bot, and regular users must have bot use access.

When a maintenance restart is pending (an update parked until the org's
maintenance window), a plain pod delete would recreate the pod from the *old*
spec: the user would pay for a disruptive restart and still get a second one
when the window opens. So the restart instead applies the pending update now,
immediately, through the same provisioner path as the admin "apply pending
restart" action. An explicit restart already accepts interrupting an active
turn, which is why this uses the immediate (no drain) apply.

patch.description:
Update bot config: persist, return, and trigger reconcile in the background.

Validation is synchronous — an invalid patch, or a config incompatible with
the bot's pinned OpenClaw version, still fails here with a 422. The bridge
*push* is not: the config is persisted with a bumped ``config_generation``
and the provisioner's config reconciler delivers it.

That split is deliberate. A bridge config apply restarts the bot's OpenClaw
process (see ``patch_and_persist_async``), so the previous push-first
behaviour made every individual settings edit cost a full restart inside the
request. Deferring lets the UI stage a batch of edits and converge them in
one restart. Callers that need the bridge's runtime verdict inline use
``patch_and_push`` instead.

Deferring the push is **not** the same as waiting for the next sweep, and the
difference is the whole user-visible latency of a settings change. Like the
skill and tool assignment routes (``bot_skills._commit_and_notify``), we
commit and then nudge the provisioner immediately, in the background: the
response is not held open for the reconcile, but reconciliation starts now
rather than whenever the reconciler next happens to look. The sweep remains
the fallback if the trigger fails, so this is a latency optimisation and not
a correctness dependency.

Only a real change is notified. ``patch_and_persist_async`` returns ``None``
for a value-preserving patch, which bumps no generation — triggering a
reconcile for it would ask the provisioner to converge state that already
matches.

post.description:
End a guided-setup bot's onboarding (the user-facing "skip setup" action).

The human equivalent of the bot-driven ``finish_onboarding`` MCP tool: flips
``onboarding_state`` pending -> complete so the chat service stops injecting
the onboarding directive, and unassigns the onboarding-only skill + tool.
Idempotent — a no-op when the bot is not pending.

Set desired_state=suspended and enqueue reconcile notification.

Gated on bot ownership, matching ``delete_bot`` rather than the looser
can-use ladder of ``restart_bot``: restarting a bot is a recovery action
that returns it to the state its users expect, while suspending it takes
the bot away from every one of them until an owner brings it back.

Idempotent — suspending an already-suspended bot returns the bot unchanged
and skips the provisioner notification.

Set desired_state=running for a suspended bot and enqueue reconcile.

A bot that is not suspended is returned unchanged: resume is the inverse of
suspend, not a general "force this bot back to running" lever.

post.description:
Revoke devices. *** THE BOT IS NOT TOUCHED. ***

This is the stolen-laptop path. Revoking denies the device on its next
assertion exchange and leaves the bot, its conversations, its memory and
its task history entirely intact — which is why revocation targets a
device and not a bot.

Idempotent: revoking an already-revoked device is a no-op that leaves the
original ``revoked_at`` in place, and is still audited, because a repeated
revoke attempt is itself worth seeing.

get.description:
List the caller's non-deleted MCP servers in this org, with Composio health re-checked.

Not "the org's servers" — servers are private. ``visible_to`` narrows the
result to what the policy engine's collection answer admits for this actor,
which for an org owner (who holds the ``mcp_server.manage`` bypass) is still
everything, and for everyone else is their memberships.

The listing is also where Composio revalidation happens (#2689), and that
is a cost decision rather than a convenience. A background sweep over every
org's connections is work a shared service pays for tenants nobody is
looking at, against a Composio control-plane bucket shared org-wide;
revalidating where somebody is actually looking scales with viewers
instead, and ``REVALIDATE_INTERVAL`` keeps a held refresh key from meaning a
vendor call per render. See :meth:`ComposioConnectService.revalidate`.

An empty body returns the first page of everything visible. This is the only

was removed once it had no callers, because its cost grew with the whole
platform catalogue rather than with the caller. Keep any future listing
route paginated in SQL. See ``core/src/botyard_core/filters/AGENTS.md`` for
the ``where`` wire format and ``McpCatalogFilterField`` for the filterable
fields.

get.description: Inspect an enabled, tenant-visible catalogue creation contract without side effects.

schema.title: Response Get Mcp Catalog Entry V1 Orgs  Org Id  Mcp Servers Catalog  Mcp Catalog Entry Id  Get

post.description:
Start authorising a Composio tile; the server is created only once it succeeds.

Gated on ``_MCP_CREATE`` rather than a read permission because that is what
this eventually does: a caller who can start a flow can complete it into an
installed MCP server, so the permission is the one for the outcome, not the
one for the first step.

Note what the request body cannot influence. The callback Composio is given
is composed inside the service from the deployment's ``app_base_url`` and a
fixed path; nothing forwarded from here reaches it — ``display_name``
included, which never leaves Botyard and is read only as the name of the
server the successful authorisation installs.

409 when the org already has a server under that name. That is the same
answer every other MCP create gives a duplicate name, and it is given here,
at the start, rather than after the customer has been to the vendor.

404 when ``mcp_connect_request_id`` names no ask this org made for this
catalogue entry. That id decides which bot is told the tile landed and in
which conversation, so it is checked against the caller's own org rather than
trusted — and rejected rather than dropped, because an attempt that settles
and tells nobody is the defect #2802 exists to remove.

502 ``integration_provider_error`` when the integration provider refuses or
cannot be reached (#3192), and 409 ``integration_setup_in_progress`` when a
concurrent request is still setting up the org's provider account — the
app tells that apart from a name collision by ``error_code``, not status.

The caller is resolved and passed down so a human starting an install is
recorded as the connecting user (D8, epic #2672) and ends up on the created
server's member list. A bot caller records nobody here — since #2688 it may
be handing the link to somebody else to authorise, and the poll is where
that person is first seen.

get.description:
The fields this tile's install form must render, read live from the vendor.

Gated on ``_MCP_CREATE`` rather than the catalogue's read permission, and
declared as a ``GET`` that is **not** a pure read. Both are deliberate:
serving this provisions the org's Composio project, because the project is
what the catalogue read authenticates as. Provisioning is idempotent and the
install that follows needs it anyway, so the alternative — a shared
Botyard-owned project in front of every tenant's form — would put one
vendor rate-limit bucket in front of every customer, which is the
noisy-neighbour shape this platform cannot afford.

404 when the entry is not visible to this org; 422 when it is not a
credential-form tile, which is the honest answer for a hosted-OAuth tile
whose customer belongs at ``POST /connections`` instead.

Nothing in the response is a credential — it is the vendor's public
description *of* one. See ``ComposioCredentialForm`` for why it is not read
from the catalogue row.

post.description:
Install an API-key tile from credentials the customer just typed.

The counterpart to ``POST /connections`` rather than a mode of it, and the
difference is visible in the response: there is no ``redirect_url`` and
nothing to poll. Composio's direct create settles in its own response, so a
201 here means the tile **exists** — ``status`` is ``connected`` and
``mcp_server_id`` is populated — where a 201 there means an attempt has
started. A client that treated the two as one shape would wait for a
completion that already happened.

Same ``_MCP_CREATE`` permission, for the same reason: this installs an MCP
server, so the permission is the one for the outcome.

422 when the values do not satisfy the vendor's live spec, and the message
names the offending fields by their **display names** — derived from the
spec, which is public, never from the vendor's error body, which on this
endpoint can echo the request that produced it. 409 when the org already has
a server under that name, answered before any vendor object or vault entry
is minted.

``body.values`` is credential material. It is not logged here and is not
logged downstream; the only thing that reaches a log line is the set of
field *names*.

``body.vault_entry_refs`` names existing Runtime Vault entries to use
instead of typed values (#3011). A signed-in person needs
``secret:secret_policy.update``. A bot needs, for every entry it names, the
access it would need to lease that entry itself — linked to it or open to
all bots, and not expired. An API key is refused. 403 when the caller may
not use vault secrets at all; 422, identical in every case, when an id is
not a live entry this org owns *or* is one the bot could not lease. Each
reference is audited in the org's vault access log, under the bot's id when
a bot made it.

get.description:
Poll one authorisation, advancing it as far as the vendor's answer allows.

Not a pure read, which is why it carries the create permission: reaching
``connected`` is what creates the MCP server, and the deadline is enforced
here too. Polling is how the install completes at all — the browser
callback is a convenience, and a claim from an untrusted browser is not
something an install may be built on.

It is also where the requesting bot is told its tile landed (#2802), for the
same reason: this is the only place an authorisation becomes an install, so
it is the only place that fact exists to be reported. The claim below is what
makes it happen once — every subsequent poll of a settled attempt sees the
same ``connected``, so "did I settle this" is not answerable from this
request alone.

delete.description:
Abandon an authorisation and clean up the vendor objects it created.

Returns the settled row rather than 204 so the caller sees the terminal
state it landed in without a follow-up poll.

get.description:
What became of one in-chat connect ask — the card's read when it mounts.

This is the read that ends the amnesia. The block in the transcript is
immutable and carries only the ask, so a reopened card resolves its
``request_id`` here and renders whatever it currently is: a completed
authorisation naming the tile, an abandoned attempt to resume polling, or the
plain form nobody has acted on yet.

**A pure read, deliberately.** It does not poll the vendor and settles
nothing — ``get_status`` stays the sole settling authority, and a lookup that
advanced state would be a second one, reachable by anyone who merely scrolled
past a card. Resuming an abandoned attempt means the card starts polling
``get_status`` again; this only tells it there is something to poll.

Gated on the same permission as starting an attempt, not a weaker read: the
question it answers is "should this reader be offered the connect button, or
told what already happened", and both halves belong to whoever may install
the tile. A reader without it sees the card's inert fallback.

Note what is absent, here as everywhere else: no ``redirect_url``. Resuming
an attempt is resuming its poll, never recovering its link.

post.description:
Offer the repair for a connection whose authorisation was revoked (#2689).

A ``POST`` under the connection rather than a second ``/connections``
create, because it is not one: no tile is installed by this, no name is
chosen, and the row it acts on already exists. The response is the same
shape a fresh start returns — a redirect to send the customer to, and the
handle to poll — because to the browser the round trip is identical, and
the poll is literally the same endpoint.

The same gate as editing the tile's credential
(``PUT /{mcp_server_id}/composio-credentials``), resolved through the
connection to the server it installed: visible, and ``mcp_server.update`` on
*that* server. Re-pointing a credential is the same act whichever route
does it, and with servers private an org-level permission would let a
non-member re-point a tile they cannot see. 404 for a connection that is
not this org's or that installed nothing; 422 when the connection is not
degraded — a healthy one has nothing to repair, and reconnecting it would
swap a working account for a pending one.

get.description:
What this tile's credential section should render, and whether it is editable.

Gated on ``mcp_server.update`` rather than a read permission, deliberately.
It is a read, but the only thing it is for is the form beside it, and the
field list plus which fields are set is a description of a live credential's
*shape* — the kind of thing to show whoever may change it and nobody else.
Composed with ``_require_visible_mcp_server`` like every other route on this
prefix, so org-wide permission still cannot reach a server the caller cannot
see.

Not a pure ``GET``, for the reason the install form's route gives: serving
it reads the vendor's live field spec, which authenticates as the org's
Composio project and therefore provisions one if the org has none.

200 with ``editable: false`` for a server this flow does not own — an OAuth
tile, a plain remote server — rather than a 404 or a 422, so the
Configuration tab can ask about any server it is rendering without branching
on error codes to decide whether to draw a section.

**No credential is returned.** The response says which fields exist and
which have a stored value. For a credential it never carries a value, a
mask, a prefix or a length. The one exception (#3044) is a field that is
plainly not a credential, such as a workspace URL, and is not linked to a
vault entry. Its stored value comes back in ``value`` so the form can show
it. That is safe to hand to exactly the audience this route already admits:
anyone with ``mcp_server.update`` can overwrite the value anyway. The rule
is ``may_display_stored_value``, and each value shown is an audited vault
read.

put.description:
Replace the vendor credential behind an installed Composio tile.

``PUT`` and not ``PATCH``, even though a partial submission is the ordinary
case. What happens downstream is a whole-credential replacement — Composio
has no in-place update, so the connection is rebuilt from the complete field
set — and the fields the customer left blank are filled from Botyard's own
stored copy rather than left alone at the vendor. ``PATCH`` would describe
the form accurately and the effect misleadingly.

The tile's endpoint URL does not change and no bot is disturbed: the Tool
Router session is re-pinned onto the new connected account in place, so
there is nothing to reconcile and no pod to bounce. Returns the refreshed
state so the form can redraw its "set" indicators without a second request.

422 when the tile is not editable this way, when nothing non-blank was
submitted, when a name is not in the vendor's spec, or when a required field
has neither a stored value nor a submitted one — always naming fields by
their display names from the public spec, never from a vendor error body,
which on this path can echo the credential that produced it.

``body.values`` is credential material. It is not logged here and not
downstream; only the set of field *names* reaches a log line.

``body.vault_entry_refs`` follows the install endpoint's rules exactly: a
person needs ``secret:secret_policy.update``, a bot needs lease access to
every entry it names, and one uniform 422 covers any id that is not a live
entry this org owns or that the bot could not lease.

A non-blank ``body.values`` entry for a field currently linked to a vault
secret replaces that link with a typed copy, so it needs the vault's own
value-write gate, ``secret:secret_policy.update`` — the same gate as
``PATCH /vault-entries/{id}``. Without it: one uniform 403 that never says
whether the linked entry still exists. A field is linked while Botyard holds
the value it took from that entry, which is exactly when the state read
reports its ``source_vault_entry_id``. Once a disconnect has deleted that
value, anyone who may edit the server can type a new one.

get.description: Return a single MCP server's full config + cached tool list.

schema.title: Response Get Mcp Server V1 Orgs  Org Id  Mcp Servers  Mcp Server Id  Get

patch.description:
Patch mutable fields; reconciler-relevant changes bump ``config_generation``.

Only fields the client actually includes are changed: we forward ``UNSET``
for omitted fields so an omitted field is never mistaken for an edit. The
nullable ``description`` / ``command`` / ``args`` clear when sent an
explicit ``null``.

Org-level **access mode is deliberately not patchable here** (epic #2672
D10). It is not a configuration field: it decides who reaches the server,
which is the member list's question, and this route's ``mcp_server.update``
gate is org-wide where that question's authority is per-instance. It lives
on ``PUT /{mcp_server_id}/access`` instead, beside the member routes, under
the same authority they use.

schema.title: Response Update Mcp Server V1 Orgs  Org Id  Mcp Servers  Mcp Server Id  Patch

delete.description:
Soft-delete — sets ``desired_state=deleted`` so the reconciler tears the pod down.

Any connection this server was granted is revoked as part of the delete, so
the acting actor is resolved here rather than discarded: a revocation is an
authorization write and is attributed like one.

get.description:
Return per-bot coverage of this server's tools, for every bot in the org.

Bot-first: the bot is the subject and this server's tools are the object.
Bots holding nothing are included — that is how the caller offers a grant to
a bot that has never used this server.

Two gates, because two different things are being read. ``BOT/TOOL/READ``
is the capability for the *data returned* (bot↔tool assignments); it is not
MCP-server read, which is merely the pivot axis. But the server is also a
resource in its own right now that membership is per-server, so
``_require_visible_mcp_server`` resolves it from the path as well —
otherwise a caller holding org-wide tool read but no membership on a
*private* server could enumerate which bots reach it.

The server is resolved first so an id belonging to another org 404s here
rather than returning an empty-but-successful assignment list, which would
confirm the id exists.

post.description:
Force a ``tools/list`` re-handshake by bumping ``config_generation``.

The reconciler (Phase 4) picks up the generation change and re-queries
the MCP server. This endpoint only nudges the generation — it doesn't
wait for the handshake to complete.

schema.title: Response Refresh Mcp Server Tools V1 Orgs  Org Id  Mcp Servers  Mcp Server Id  Refresh Tools Post

post.description:
Re-enter the reconciler queue for a FAILED MCP server.

Resets the row to ``observed_state=pending``, clears ``last_error`` and
any stuck operator lease, and bumps ``config_generation`` so the
provisioner treats it as drift-to-apply on the next sweep. Returns
``409 Conflict`` when the row is not currently FAILED — re-entering a
healthy or in-flight row would fight the reconciler's own lease and
leak confusing errors back to the operator.

schema.title: Response Restart Mcp Server V1 Orgs  Org Id  Mcp Servers  Mcp Server Id  Restart Post

put.description:
Set who reaches this server org-wide: its members only, or everybody.

Its own route rather than a field on ``PATCH`` (epic #2672 D10), because the
authority differs. ``PATCH`` is gated on org-wide ``mcp_server.update``,
which only an org owner holds; who reaches a server is the *member list's*
question, and Unit 3's whole premise is that a plain ``org:member`` can own
an MCP server and govern it. Putting the mode on the patch body would have
meant an instance owner could add and remove members — deciding reach one
principal at a time — and could not decide it for the org, which is the same
authority with a harder path.

So this sits beside the member routes and takes their gate, via
``_require_editable_member_list``: instance ``owner``, or the listing rule's
administrative bypass. ``PUT`` because the body is the desired state of one
value and sending it twice changes nothing the first send did not.

``open`` is wider than it sounds and the response is the whole server, so a
caller sees what it actually did: every principal in the org holding
``mcp_server.read`` reaches an open server — every member *and viewer*,
every bot, and every API key. The transition is written to the audit trail
before the row moves.

schema.title: Response Set Mcp Server Access V1 Orgs  Org Id  Mcp Servers  Mcp Server Id  Access Put

get.description:
Who reaches this MCP server, owners first.

Readable by anyone who can see the server, not only by owners. A member who
cannot see the list cannot tell whether they are looking at a server nobody
owns or one they should be asking somebody about — and "who do I ask" is the
question a member list is most often opened to answer.

schema.title: Response List Mcp Server Members V1 Orgs  Org Id  Mcp Servers  Mcp Server Id  Members Get

put.description:
Put a principal on the member list, or change the role it holds.

``PUT`` rather than ``POST`` because the operation is idempotent: the body
describes the desired state of one membership, and sending it twice leaves
the same single row. That is what makes D7's remedy — *an owner re-adds the
person the backfill stranded* — safe to hand to somebody as an instruction.

Both validators in :mod:`botyard_core.authz.membership` run before anything
is written, and both surface here as ``422`` rather than as a stored row:
an undeclared role matches no predicate, and an undeclared *actor type* is
worse — it inserts cleanly, renders in this list, and grants nothing.

Two authorities, not one. ``_require_editable_member_list`` answers *may you
touch this list*; :func:`may_confer_member_role` answers *may you hand out
this particular role*, which became a separate question the moment a role
started carrying permissions. Together they mean an instance owner can
appoint a co-owner, and a narrowly-granted administrator who holds only
``mcp_server.manage`` can add members but cannot mint an owner and thereby
confer the ``update`` and ``delete`` it does not hold.

schema.title: Response Add Mcp Server Member V1 Orgs  Org Id  Mcp Servers  Mcp Server Id  Members Put

delete.description:
Take a principal off the member list.

The principal is addressed by both axes in the path, because ``actor_id``
alone does not say which population it is drawn from — and removing the wrong
one would be a silent no-op rather than an error.

Removing the **last owner** is refused with ``409`` and the remedy named:
a list with no owner can then only be repaired by someone holding org-wide
authority, on a resource whose entire point is that an ``org:member`` can own
one without it.

get.description: List all Runtime Vault entries for the organization with linked-bot counts.

post.description:
Create a Runtime Vault entry and store its encrypted plaintext value.

Ensures an org keypair exists (creates one if not). Plaintext value is
encrypted immediately and never returned in responses.

Key paths in a Botyard-reserved namespace are refused; the error names the
reserved prefix.

post.description:
Overwrite several Runtime Vault entries' values in one transaction.

All or nothing: every entry is resolved before any is written, and one
unknown entry, expired entry or refused value rolls every write back. An
unknown id, another org's entry and a reserved entry all get the same 404,
which names none of them. Each write queues its Composio re-push in the same
transaction, so a tile linking several of these entries is only ever pushed
all of the new values together (task 3016). Same permission as a single
``PATCH``; metadata and each entry's expiry are unchanged.

get.description:
List the Composio tiles holding a linked copy of a Runtime Vault entry.

Editing the entry re-pushes its value to each of them; deleting it
disconnects them. Gated like ``bot-links``: it names consumers, never values.

cold-start snapshot of which conversations are currently streaming. The
chat message list exposes this per conversation; this bulk endpoint applies
the same lease TTL and conversation visibility rules.

With ``all_visible=True`` the caller gets every active turn it can see and
filters locally — preferred for the chat polls, which watch an unbounded
number of conversations but only ever see a small set of live streams.
Otherwise the result is narrowed to the requested ``conversation_ids``
and/or ``bot_slugs`` (OR-combined).

patch.description:
Change a conversation's access scope (publish to org / make private).

Only the conversation **owner** (its creator) may change its scope — not org
owners. Privatizing returns a conversation to its owner, so letting a
non-owner do it would just remove their own access; and force-publishing
would expose someone's private conversation. Ownerless (integration/bot/
API-key) conversations cannot be privatized, and API keys can never move a
conversation to user-scope.

post.description:
Continue privately: fork a readable conversation into a new private one.

Creates a **user-scoped** conversation with the same bot, owned by the
caller, holding a copy of the source transcript, its attachments and — the
part that makes it a true fork — the bot's own memory of it (its context
ledger). The bot in the copy cannot tell it from the source. Nothing is
sent to the bot and the source is only read: nothing is written or
announced there.

Native bots only: other bots keep their history in their own runtime, so
the endpoint answers 409 and the client offers a new empty private
conversation instead. Also 409 (retryable) while the bot is still working
in the source.

Access: the caller must be able to read the source (scope + bot use) and
hold ``conversation:create`` for its bot. Only users may fork — the fork is
private and needs a human owner. A fork is a copy, not a share, so it never
widens who can see anything; it does outlive later changes to the source.
Append a message to a conversation.

List messages in a conversation, cursor-paginated.

Without a cursor, returns the newest ``limit`` messages. With
``before_ordinal``, returns the newest ``limit`` older than the cursor.
Items are always returned ASC for chronological display.

The response also carries ``active_turn`` — the conversation's
actively-streaming turn (or null), so a cold-start client can resume an
in-flight stream from its seq watermark instead of replaying realtime
history.

post.description:
Delete, edit, regenerate or reset messages: both views, all or nothing (#3818).

One command, two views (#3732 §3): ``conversation_messages`` (what users
see) and the context ledger (what the model sees) change in one
transaction, or the request is refused and neither changes. Removed rows
are kept and marked, never hard-deleted.

- ``delete``: tombstones each message in the ledger; a reply takes its
  whole turn.
- ``edit_sent``: branches before the message, then sends the edited copy
  as a new turn. Only its sender may edit it.
- ``regenerate``: branches before the reply. It does not start a turn.
- ``reset``: branches before the message.

Deleting, regenerating and resetting need an org owner, or the owner of a
private conversation. Bots and API keys are refused. Every request writes
one audit event.

Refused with 409 while a turn is running or queued
(``transcript_turn_in_flight``), when a message has no single counterpart
in the model's history (``transcript_message_unmappable``), or when it was
already removed (``transcript_message_already_removed``).

get.summary: Mint a fresh download URL for one file of a ``files`` content block
get.description:
Return a short-lived download URL for a file a bot sent via ``send_files``.

Authorization is layered: ``conversation:content_block.read`` names the
capability (and brings org membership + org MFA with it), while
``require_conversation_access`` confines the read to a conversation this
viewer can actually see. The sibling payload/task routes enforce only the
latter because they predate the named-permission migration.

The URL is **minted per request** rather than persisted on the block. A
presigned URL stored in tool-return metadata would go stale — the message read
path re-signs user-prompt parts and the ``media`` column, not tool returns — so
a block that carried its own URLs would rot into dead links. The filename,
content type, and size come from object metadata rather than the request, so a
crafted link can't change what a viewer sees or downloads.

get.summary: Read a board-task content block's current (live) state
get.description:
Return a board-task content block's **current** renderable state.

The durable ``task`` block carries only a reference (``workforce_slug`` +
``task_number``); this endpoint resolves the task's protected content on
demand so the renderer can draw the live card. Because the content lives only
here — behind the membership gate — and never in the conversation payload, a
conversation-reader who isn't a board member cannot obtain it.

Authorization is layered:

- ``require_conversation_access`` confines the read to a conversation the
  viewer can see — the same surface guard as the sibling payload route.
- **Workforce membership** is the task's own read-access rule (the VIEW
  claim ``get_task`` / ``get_workforce`` enforce). A viewer with
  conversation access but no board access gets ``403`` — the renderer maps
  that to a "no access / unavailable" card, exactly like a linked
  conversation the viewer can't see. A missing/deleted task or board is
  ``404``.

The state shares the reference fields with the inline block (both via
``botyard_core.services.api.task_block``), so the card resolves crumb,
deeplink, and content from this single fetch.

Save this respondent's draft answers, enforcing the per-field revision check.

Called on every debounced edit, so it is deliberately cheap and partial: it
stores drafts, never submits, and never wakes the bot. A stale
``expected_revision`` returns 409 naming the field to re-read.

post.description:
Finalize this respondent's answers and wake the bot once with them.

Saves any answers carried in the body, checks every required field is
answered, marks this respondent's answers final under a row lock (one-shot per
person, not per question), commits, and schedules a single wake naming the
respondent. Other respondents' drafts are untouched and the question stays
open — closing it is the bot's decision, because only the bot knows how many
answers it needed.

get.description: Return an approval's live state as this viewer sees it.

post.description:
Approve or deny a bot's request to spend the organization's money.

Approving issues a short-lived, single-use grant bound to the digest of the
payload on the card; the bot is woken with that payload handed back to it and
retries the same call, which now passes the gate. The wake echoes the payload
rather than relying on the bot to remember it, because the default approval
lifetime is seven days and the asking session is usually long gone by the time
a human answers. Denying issues nothing and tells the bot why.

Three refusals sit in front of the transition, in this order:

1. **Authority.** The decider must hold the permission the kind's own action
   requires, over and above the ``conversation:approval.update`` floor the
   route already gated on. A member who could not create the MCP server
   themselves cannot authorize a bot to create it for them — that is the
   whole sentence the actor rule is built around.
2. **Hard cap.** A grant cannot buy past a plan limit, so approving one that
   the cap already blocks would mint authority for a call that is going to be
   refused anyway. Refused as ``plan_limit_reached``, the same code the gate
   would raise.
3. **Payment method.** On a card-free org a chargeable approval cannot be
   granted, so the request is left ``pending`` and an activation intent is
   returned for the client's existing checkout flow. See
   :class:`~botyard_api.models.approvals.ApprovalActivationIntent` for why
   there is no "approved, awaiting payment" state.

Denials skip 2 and 3 entirely: refusing to spend money is always available,
whatever the plan says.

**Payload-dependent authority (#3157).** A kind may add an
``approver_shortfall`` hook on top of the static permission; an approve is
refused while it names anything. For ``bot_tool.assign`` that is the union
of the listed tools' requirements plus their visibility to the approver.

**Kinds performed on approval.** For a ``performed_on_approval`` kind the
action happens here, in the decision's transaction, and its grant is spent
by id before commit — the bot is told it is done rather than to retry. A
failure anywhere rolls the decision back with it, so the request stays
pending and nothing is half-applied.

get.description: Return the live status of a vault input request group (never any value).

post.description:
Store the user-supplied secret value(s) for a request group and wake the bot.

Locks the whole pending group (one-shot), re-checks conflicts at each (possibly
user-edited) key, then for every secret either creates a new bot-owned secret or
— when the secret opted into ``allow_update`` and the requesting bot is already
authorized for the existing key — replaces just that key's value, all in one
transaction; marks the group submitted; and schedules a single post-commit wake.
Submission is **all-or-nothing** and must cover exactly the secrets in the group;
the values are never logged or echoed back.

Any user with conversation access may fulfill the request for the requesting
bot. **Broadening** the secrets to other bots or all bots is a cross-bot
distribution decision — owner-gated exactly like the normal secret modal — so
``bot_ids``/``allow_all_bots`` require org-owner role. The pending request only
authorizes storing the secrets for the bot that asked.

Send a chat message; bot response arrives over Centrifugo.

``mode=steer`` injects the message into the active turn instead of queueing
it behind one (no-op if no turn is active). Default ``queue`` preserves the
prior ordering behaviour.

Wake an idle conversation with a hidden developer message.

Starts a bot turn carrying the message as system context — invisible in
the chat UI but read by the bot's model. Intended for automations
(webhooks, schedulers, polling processes) that need to nudge a bot
without keeping a session open. If the conversation already has a
running or queued turn, nothing is sent and status is 'already_active'.

Promote an already-queued message to steer.

Forwards a steer signal to the bot, which pulls the queued message out of
its ordering gate and injects it into the active turn. Whether the message
is still queued (vs. already dispatched) is decided by the bot, which
no-ops if the steer arrived too late.

``require_conversation`` enforces access and hands us the row, so we reuse
its ``bot_id`` instead of re-fetching the conversation.

Cancel an already-queued message before it runs.

Forwards a cancel signal to the bot, which pulls the queued message out of
its ordering gate and drops it so it never runs (the proxy then marks the
turn ``cancelled``). Whether the message is still queued (vs. already
dispatched) is decided by the bot, which no-ops if the cancel arrived too
late.

``require_conversation`` enforces access and hands us the row, so we reuse
its ``bot_id`` instead of re-fetching the conversation.

Edit an already-queued message's content (text and/or attachments).

Locates the queued turn by ``request_id`` and rewrites its content in place —
the bot swaps the queued payload in its ordering gate so the new content is
what dispatches, and the persisted row is updated so the transcript matches.
Returns 409 when the message is no longer queued (already dispatched or
dismissed) or the bot has no live connection; the edit is a safe no-op in
that case.

post.description:
What each connection of these pack versions needs, before any bot exists (P3.4).

Per connection: what connecting a new account takes (`setup`, decided by
the same rule as the setup engine), whether a new server is metered, and
the org's existing servers from that catalogue entry that you may see, each
with its account, owner, access, the bots using it and its health. Bots you

called.

reads the same ids' contents.

What installing would do, per bot. Nothing is written.

Per install: each item (`add`, `adopt`, `unsupported`, `pending`), each
connection and the servers it could bind, runtime `support`, and the pack's
recommended model as a suggestion. Refused (422/403) exactly as the install
would be.

**Turned off for now:** installing onto an existing bot would replace its
soul, so this is refused with a 409 `pack_install_existing_bot_disabled`,
as the install is, until multi-pack installs and soul merging land.
Create a bot from the pack instead (`POST /bots/from-pack`).

Bind installs' connections to an MCP server or the org's vault entry: all or none.

Name `mcp_server_id` when several of the entry's servers fit; omit it to
bind the one that does. Each MCP binding reports the pack tools the server
has not discovered yet (`missing_tools`).
What uninstalling would remove, restore or keep, per install. Nothing is written.

Every connection of these installs, and what its setup asks next.

Binds what has become bindable (a secret now stored, a server the org
made, an authorisation that settled, tools now discovered). Never creates a
server or calls a vendor. Each setup commits on its own.

Carry setups forward with no human input: each one, independently.

Creates the MCP server as the caller (the capacity gate and its approvals
apply), starts a vendor authorisation (its `connect` link is returned once,
to this call only), or retries a failed step. Not all-or-nothing: each
setup committed on its own. Needs `mcp_server.create`, as creating the
server or starting its sign-in directly does.

Apply what a human supplied (form answers, vendor credentials, a server choice).

Each completion must be of the kind its setup asks for, or nothing is done.
Credential values go to the vendor and are never stored or logged here;
naming vault entries instead needs `secret:secret_policy.update`. Each
setup commits on its own.

A form or credential completion carries the setup on into creating the
server or starting its sign-in, so it needs `mcp_server.create`; without it
the whole batch is refused (403) before anything is done. A server choice
only binds an existing server and needs no more than the pack write gates.

Exchange a signed device assertion for a short-lived runtime session.

The device registry is read live on every call and a device that is not
active is refused here, before its signature is even examined. There is no
cache, no TTL and no memoised lookup between that row and this decision,
and there must never be one: it is the only reason a credential that never
expires can still be revoked.

Exchange a scheduled pod's JWT-SVID for a short-lived runtime session.

The pod twin of :func:`exchange_device_assertion`: no enrollment token,
no device key, no custody row. Attestation is the SVID itself, verified
against the SPIRE OIDC discovery JWKS; the entry that lets SPIRE mint it
is the scope control. Each SVID buys exactly one session (replay loses on
the session row's unique index), so a pod fetches fresh per exchange and
entry deletion stops new sessions within one SVID lifetime.

Redeem an enrollment token, registering this machine as the bot's device.

Registering the public key and consuming the token are atomic: the token
is spent by a conditional UPDATE that exactly one concurrent caller can
win, and the device row is written in the same transaction, so a token is
never consumed without producing the device it paid for.

No session, assertion or SVID is issued here. The device credential buys
only the right to *ask* for one, on every future connection, against a
registry that can deny it immediately.

*** THERE IS EXACTLY ONE WAY TO LEAVE HERE WITHOUT A DEVICE ROW, AND IT IS
AN ERROR. *** A 2xx from this endpoint means the registry holds a live,
active device for the caller — either written by this call (``201``,
``newly_enrolled``) or read back within it (``200``, the machine already
being that device and offering its key). The caller may therefore treat
"this call succeeded" as "a device exists server-side", which is the
property an installer needs and the one it cannot establish for itself.

get.description:
Active task counts per column, for every board in the org the caller may view.

Exists because there was no way to answer "how are this board's tasks
distributed across its columns" without listing the tasks themselves. The
task list caps ``limit`` at 100, so the largest board in production (2002
tasks, 6.6 MB of title and description text) needs 21 pages to be counted
client-side; asking per column instead trades that for one request per
(board, column), which on the same org is 53 requests. Both are worse than
a single indexed aggregate, which is what this is.

The collision with ``/{workforce_slug}`` is guarded twice, and the order
matters. **First**, ``RESERVED_WORKFORCE_SLUGS`` refuses this slug on
create and on update, so no board can newly reach it — relying on route
order alone would let an authorised editor create a board that is then
reachable at neither its detail GET nor its PATCH, which is worse than the
ambiguity it avoids. **Second**, this route is still registered ahead of
``/{workforce_slug}`` so the aggregate wins for legacy rows and for values
written straight to the database, which the service layer never sees. That
ordering is the same trade ``/tasks/tags`` already makes against
``/tasks/{task_id}``; the difference is that here it is the fallback rather
than the only defence.

Get a workforce by slug.

A bot can only get a board it is a member of; any other slug is reported
as not found.

One group per requested skill, in request order. Same visibility as reading
each skill: a member- or bot-scoped skill the caller cannot see counts as
unknown. All-or-nothing: any unknown slug fails the request with 404, naming
it. ``pinnable`` says whether a bot may be pinned to the version (see
``PUT /bots/{bot_slug}/skills/pins``).

``limit`` and ``offset`` apply to every skill. The whole response is capped
at 500 versions, so the applied per-skill ``limit`` may be lower than
requested; it is echoed. To page further into one skill, request it alone.

Resolve a source reference without installing anything.

Gated on SKILL.CREATE rather than SKILL.READ: this reads nothing from the
catalogue. It makes the server fetch a third-party repository, which is the
privileged half of an import — so the permission that authorises the import
is the one that authorises the dry run.

The same reasoning makes the private-source capability apply here: a preview
that could read a private repository the subsequent import could not would be
a way to read private source without importing it, and one that could not
read what the import can would report "not found" for a repository that
imports fine.

Install a skill from a GitHub or skills.sh reference.

The caller sends a reference, not the skill — which is the whole point.
Sending content through a request body is what forced a bot to shorten a
skill until it fit, and a larger skill would simply have failed.

A private repository additionally needs ``skill:private_source.create``; a
caller without it gets exactly today's behaviour, including today's message,
which the source of a private repository makes true rather than a guess.

Re-pull an imported skill from its source, keeping its identity.

Without this, changing a pin from ``v1`` to ``v2`` can only be done by
deleting the skill and importing it again — which mints a new skill id and
breaks every bot assignment that referenced the old one. Here the row is
updated in place, so the id and its assignments survive a version bump.

Gated on SKILL.CREATE rather than SKILL.UPDATE for the same reason
``/import/preview`` is: this makes the server fetch a third-party
repository and install what it finds, which is an import, not an edit.

Returns 200 either way. When the source resolves to the commit already
recorded, nothing is written and the unchanged skill comes back — so a
reconcile loop can call this on every pass. Compare ``source.commit_sha``
to see whether anything moved.

The private-source capability is consulted here too, and it has to be: a
refresh re-fetches the repository, so a skill imported from a private source
would otherwise be permanently un-refreshable, and the caller who *can*
import privately would be told their own skill's source no longer exists. It
is consulted per call rather than inherited from the original import, so
revoking the permission stops future refreshes and does not need a sweep of
previously imported rows.

Explain a candidate spec as concrete upcoming instants. Persists nothing.

Exists because a cron expression is unreadable: the edit dialog needs to
show *when this will actually fire* for a spec the user is still typing, and
a saved schedule's ``next_fire_at`` can only answer that for one occurrence
of an already-saved row.

Answering server-side is a deliberate choice over parsing cron in the
browser. This shares :func:`compute_next_fire_ats` — and therefore
``croniter`` and ``ZoneInfo`` — with the ``next_fire_at`` every read already
derives, so the preview cannot disagree with the schedule it is previewing.
A second, client-side implementation would have to re-solve DST, and would
be wrong twice a year in a way nothing here would catch.

An unparseable spec is a 4xx (the same ``SpecValidationError`` mapping the
write paths use), which lets a half-typed cron expression be reported as
invalid rather than as "no upcoming runs".

get.description:

A command run nests every attempt (retries and "not ready" rechecks), so a
run that rechecked 13 times is one entry, not 14. Runs are a union on
`kind`: `prompt`, `command`, or `command_unstarted` (a command occurrence
that never started a run). Each carries a normalised `status` and its raw
outcome. Pages are keyed by run, so newer runs arriving between pages never
shift them.

Prompt runs live in the scheduler's own database. When it is unavailable
the read still returns command runs, with `fire_history_available=false`.

Fire a schedule immediately (out-of-band 'run now').

Delegates to :func:`trigger_schedule_now`, the single operation shared with
the ``schedule_trigger_now`` MCP tool: it delivers the schedule's ``prompt``
as a fire-and-forget hidden wake via chat-proxy — the same path a scheduled
fire uses, without touching Prefect or the normal cadence — and appends the
``MANUAL`` history row. Returns 'already_active' when the conversation
already has a running/queued turn.

The route deliberately owns none of that sequence (task #1269): when each
surface hand-rolled it, only this one recorded, and every bot-initiated
trigger vanished from run history.

Run command schedules now (manual trigger), outside their cadence.

Each accepted item records a ``manual`` run that the scheduler-worker starts
within seconds, sharing the schedule's ``concurrency_group``, run history and
``on_outcome`` routing. Manual runs never move the schedule's failure counter
or outcome class, and a ``pause`` routed from one is ignored. Per-item
results: ``accepted`` (with ``run_id``), ``already_running`` (the lock is
held; nothing recorded) or ``rejected`` (with a reason). Accepted items
commit together.

``env_overrides`` names must be in the schedule's ``overridable_env``.
Values are stored and shown in run history: never send secrets here.

Every attempted fire is recorded — delivered, skipped, missed or failed —

History lives in ``scheduler-postgres``, a **different cluster** from the
platform database. Tenancy is therefore enforced here, before that cluster is
touched: the schedule is first resolved under this org+bot via the platform
database, so an id belonging to another tenant 404s rather than reaching the
history query. If scheduler-postgres is unavailable this returns 503

post.description:
Which permissions this tool set requires, and which the bot lacks.

**One call for the whole set.** Beyond the obvious cost saving over N calls,
a single resolution makes the answer internally consistent: N calls could
interleave with a concurrent grant and return a combination of statuses that
no single moment ever produced, which a user would then act on as a snapshot.

A ``POST`` because the tool-id set is a request body, not because it writes.
**Nothing here grants, revokes or assigns anything** — it reports. Issuance
stays in ``AuthzGrantService`` with its no-escalation, tenant-containment and
audit guarantees, and ``grantable_by_caller`` is advisory: the service
re-runs the identical ``covers`` check on the write, so a client that ignores
this answer gains nothing.

Gated on reading the bot's tools rather than on ``authz:permission.read``:
the question is *"what do these tools need?"*, asked by whoever is looking at
the tool picker. It discloses the bot's authority only as a per-requirement
satisfied/missing flag, which is strictly less than the permissions surface
already returns to a holder of that permission.

Action.title: Action
Action.description:
The verb a permission authorizes (a permission axis).

``READ`` is the sole non-mutating action; every other action mutates state
(drives the ``audit`` obligation and the bot-write guard).

**This set is deliberately small and closed.** Actions describe *kinds of
authority*; :class:`Resource` is the open axis that carries specificity.
Action-per-operation vocabularies (AWS IAM's ``s3:PutObject``) only survive
because nobody hand-maintains policies at that scale — our role bundles are
hand-maintained, and custom-role authoring is a planned product capability,
so verb proliferation would make bundles unmaintainable and turn this enum
into a mirror of the API surface.

A new action must clear **all three** tests:

1. someone would realistically grant it *independently* of neighbouring verbs;
2. it represents *materially higher trust* (typically irreversible);
3. it *cannot be expressed by splitting the resource* instead.

When in doubt, grow :class:`Resource`, not this enum.

ActiveTurnsRequest.title: ActiveTurnsRequest
ActiveTurnsRequest.description:
Request body for bulk active-turn lookup.

Two modes:

- ``all_visible=True``: return every active turn the caller can see, scoped
  only by conversation visibility. No candidate list is needed — the set of
  currently-streaming conversations is small (one short-lived lease row per
  stream), so the client can fetch the whole visible set in one request and
  filter locally. This is the mode the chat polls use, and it scales
  regardless of how many conversations a client watches.
- ``all_visible=False`` (default): narrow to the given ``conversation_ids``
  and/or ``bot_slugs`` (combined with OR). Capped per request — prefer
  ``all_visible`` for unbounded candidate sets rather than chunking.

AdminActionPerformedContent.title: AdminActionPerformedContent
AdminActionPerformedContent.description:
Typed content for a privileged ``/v1/admin`` mutation.

The **security-attribution floor** for the admin surface: emitted by the
authorization enforcement point itself whenever a mutating platform
permission is granted, so a route is audited *by virtue of being gated*
rather than by someone remembering to add a builder. That structural
property is what the interim bot-write guard's removal rests on — a
per-operation builder is something a future route can forget, and a
guarantee that depends on nobody forgetting is not a guarantee.

It records the *authorization* of the action, since the enforcement point
runs before the handler: "this principal was permitted to perform this
operation". Richer, semantically-typed events (``rollout.initiated``,
``provisioning.maintenance_restart.force_applied``,
``admin.platform_team.*``) remain the record of what the operation actually
did, and are deliberately **not** suppressed by this one — the two answer
different questions, and suppression logic is precisely what would let the
floor develop holes.

``permission`` is the canonical ``domain:resource.action`` id;
``route`` is the path *template* (never the resolved path, so ids do not
leak into the event type's shape); ``path_params`` carries the resolved
path parameters, which is what identifies the affected object.

AdminCredentialPresetPatch.title: AdminCredentialPresetPatch
AdminCredentialPresetPatch.description:
Admin request to partially update a credential provider preset.

Every field is optional and **omission is distinct from null**: an omitted
field keeps its persisted value, while an explicit ``null`` clears a
nullable one. The route reads ``model_fields_set`` (via
``exclude_unset=True``) to tell the two apart, so ``api_protocol: null``
means "this provider has no wire protocol" rather than "leave it alone".

The catalogue is edited by *operation* rather than by replacement:
``upsert_models`` adds or replaces entries by model id (in place, so display
order is stable) and ``remove_model_ids`` drops them. That is what makes
"add one model" expressible without resending the rest of the catalogue —
and therefore without a partial payload being able to silently delete it,
which the whole-object PUT cannot avoid.

AdminMcpCatalogEntryUpdatedContent.title: AdminMcpCatalogEntryUpdatedContent
AdminMcpCatalogEntryUpdatedContent.description:
Typed content for an operator edit to one MCP setup-catalogue tile.

``admin.action.performed`` already records that a principal was *authorised*
to call ``PATCH /admin/mcp-catalog/{entry_id}``. It cannot record what the
call did: the enforcement point runs before the handler and sees only the
path parameters. This event is the other half — what actually changed on the
row — and the two are deliberately both emitted.

**Why the consent note is stored in full and the rest is not.** Three of the
four override columns are product copy; knowing they moved is enough, and
keeping marketing text forever in a ``SECURITY``-retention table buys
nothing. ``operator_consent_note`` and ``operator_consent_title`` are the
exception, because together they are the text
a customer's user read before granting a third party access to their account
— and the question an incident asks about it is never "did it change" but
"what exactly did it say on the day they clicked Authorise". A ``"set"``
marker cannot answer that, and the row itself holds only the current value,
so an edit made at 3am is otherwise unreconstructable. Both sides are kept:
the previous text is the one no longer recoverable from anywhere else.

The note is capped at 4,096 characters by ``AdminMcpCatalogUpdate`` and the
title at 200, so retaining both sides is bounded. None of these fields is a
secret: this is operator-authored copy written to be shown to end users.

``*_changed`` flags rather than inferring change from inequality, so that
"the operator re-sent identical text" and "the operator did not touch this
field" remain distinguishable in the record.

'custom' is the operator writing the disclosure themselves in operator_consent_title and operator_consent_note, which then replace the platform title and paragraphs and both become required. Cannot be cleared — every tile has a shape, and 'none' is how an operator says a tile needs no warning

Checked under a row lock, so it is a true compare-and-set — for bulk tooling that must never overwrite a shape a human set between its read and its write. Absent means unconditional

AdminMcpCatalogUpdate.title: AdminMcpCatalogUpdate
AdminMcpCatalogUpdate.description:
Operator-owned catalogue state. Every field optional, absent means leave.

``extra="forbid"`` and an explicit field list rather than a generic patch:
this endpoint is the *only* write path to a catalogue row outside the
importer, and the columns it must never touch — ``endpoint_url``,
``managed_endpoint_source``, ``managed_credential_headers``,
``managed_endpoint_apps``, ``provenance``, and the vendor's own ``name`` /
``description`` / ``logo_url`` — are code-owned. An operator editing those
through this route would be silently reverted by the next import, which is
a worse failure than being refused.

**Absent is not null.** Omitting a key leaves the stored value alone;
sending ``null`` (or a blank string) clears the override and returns the
tile to the vendor's copy. Both are things an operator wants to say and a
plain optional field cannot distinguish, so the two are separated by
``model_fields_set`` at the call site rather than by sentinel values here.

AdminPlatformSkillDeleteRequest.title: AdminPlatformSkillDeleteRequest
AdminPlatformSkillDeleteRequest.description:
Delete platform skills, all or nothing (PlatDev #3637, D26).

Without ``force``, a skill any live bot holds is refused with 409
``skill_in_use``. With ``force`` ("delete anyway") and the dry run's
``expected_impact_token``, it is removed from those bots, pinned or not, and
deleted; a holder set that changed since the dry run is refused with 409
``skill_delete_impact_changed``. Protected skills (onboarding, bot
templates, skills a published pack version pins) are refused with 409
``platform_skill_protected`` either way.

AdminPlatformSkillUpdate.title: AdminPlatformSkillUpdate
AdminPlatformSkillUpdate.description:
Edit a platform skill's head. The slug is immutable.

``expected_head_version_id`` is **required** (it may be ``null`` for a skill
that has never been versioned): it is the head this edit was based on, and
a mismatch is a 409 with nothing written. ``files`` replaces the whole file
set; ``upsert_files``/``delete_files`` patch it. The two forms are mutually
exclusive. Omitted fields are left alone.

``suggested`` is catalogue metadata, not content: changing it records no
version, so the head check does not order two concurrent ``suggested``-only
edits. Each states the flag's final value explicitly and the later one
stands.

ApprovalActivationIntent.title: ApprovalActivationIntent
ApprovalActivationIntent.description:
What the client must do before this approval can be granted.

Present only when the org is on its plan's card-free variant and the ask is
chargeable. The decision route does **not** approve in that case: the
request stays ``pending`` and the client runs the existing activation
checkout, after which the human decides again on a card-bearing org.

That is a deliberate refusal to invent an intermediate state. An
"approved, pending payment" request would be a row whose status says a human
said yes while no grant exists, and the enforcement path matches grants —
not statuses — so such a row is unconsumable by construction *today* and one
careless query away from being consumable tomorrow. Not creating it is
cheaper to keep true than guarding it.

approve.title: Approve
approve.description: True to approve and issue the grant, False to deny. Deliberately a boolean on one route rather than two verbs on two routes: approve and deny are the same state transition on the same record and must race against each other, which two routes make easy to forget.

reason.title: Reason
reason.description: Optional note, carried back to the bot on the wake. A denial with a reason is worth far more to an agent than a bare no.

ApprovalDecisionRequest.title: ApprovalDecisionRequest
ApprovalDecisionRequest.description: A human's approve/deny, with an optional note.

state.description: The card's state after this call.

activation_required.description: Set when the decision was *not* applied because the organization must add a payment method first. Null on every applied decision, including every denial — denying is always free.

ApprovalDecisionResponse.title: ApprovalDecisionResponse
ApprovalDecisionResponse.description:
The outcome of a decision attempt.

Always carries the refreshed read model, so a client never has to re-fetch
to redraw the card — including in the activation case, where the state it
carries is still ``pending`` and the client can see for itself that nothing
was decided.

ApprovalKind.title: ApprovalKind
ApprovalKind.description:
Which action a bot is asking a human's permission to take.

The open axis of the approval schema, and deliberately the *only* one: each
member resolves to a registry entry in
:mod:`botyard_core.services.api.approval_kinds` supplying the typed payload
schema, the permission the approver must hold, the quote resolver, the card
presenter, and the grant issuer. Adding an approval kind is one registry
entry — no new API surface, no new tool, no new UI.

Values are dotted ``resource.action`` rather than bare verbs so a kind reads
the same as the permission it gates, and so future non-billing approvals
(the reason the mechanism is generic at all) name themselves consistently.

The metered members are exactly the bot-facing writes in
``cluster-services/botyard-mcp`` that reach
:class:`~botyard_core.services.api.gate_enforcer.GateEnforcer` — ``org``
tools expose reads only, so a bot can create neither bots nor seats.
``BOT_TOOL_ASSIGN`` and ``PERMISSION_GRANT`` are the unmetered members:
they gate authority, not spend.

tool_ids.title: Tool Ids
tool_ids.description: Every listed tool that needs it. Empty for ``permission.grant``, which asks for the permission itself rather than for tools.

grantable_by_caller.title: Grantable By Caller
grantable_by_caller.description: Whether the viewing human holds authority covering it. False means approving needs someone with more authority — the card's Approve is withheld by the same predicate.

ApprovalMissingPermission.title: ApprovalMissingPermission
ApprovalMissingPermission.description:
A permission approving a ``bot_tool.assign`` or ``permission.grant`` would grant the bot.

Shaped like the dashboard gate's ``MissingPermissionResponse`` so the same
row component renders both. Per-viewer and live — whether *this* viewer can
cover it, and whether the bot still lacks it, both change after mint — so it
lives on :class:`ApprovalRequestState`, never on the immutable spec.

item_label.title: Item Label
item_label.description: What is being bought, as a noun phrase — e.g. 'a hosted MCP server'. Matches the idiom ``ActivateBillingDialog`` already uses, so the sentence reads the same whether a human or a bot initiated it.

price_cents.title: Price Cents
price_cents.description: Recurring cost of this unit in minor units, or None when the cost is metered and cannot honestly be stated as a fixed figure up front. None renders the 'billed by usage' copy rather than a number, exactly as the human-side dialog does.

currency.title: Currency
currency.description: ISO 4217 code of ``price_cents``, from the *plan*. Carried with the amount rather than resolved by the renderer: pairing an amount with another object's currency is how a '€5' becomes a '$5'.

interval.title: Interval
interval.description: Billing interval the price recurs on, for the '/month' suffix.

meter.description: The meter this unit counts against; ties the card back to the plan gate.

included_remaining.title: Included Remaining
included_remaining.description: Units still inside the plan's included allowance. Zero — the Starter case for hosted MCP servers — means this unit is chargeable. Kept on the quote so the card can say 'your first one is included' truthfully without re-deriving the plan.

ApprovalQuote.title: ApprovalQuote
ApprovalQuote.description:
What approving this will cost, as the card states it to the human.

Resolved server-side from the plan's gate at mint time — never supplied by
the bot. A bot that could author the price on its own approval card could
understate it, and the whole point of the card is that the figure on it is
the figure that will be charged.

**``meter``, not ``meter_key``, and deliberately out of step with the rest of
the billing vocabulary.** This model is reachable from a bot-facing tool's
output schema (``request_approval`` returns
:class:`ApprovalRequestResult`), and OpenClaw's redactor masks payload fields
called ``*_key`` to ``"***"`` in the transcript Botyard persists — so a
``meter_key`` here would come back to the model as a literal ``"***"`` in its
own conversation history. ``PlanMeterGate.meter_key`` and the usage models
keep the longer name because nothing puts them in a tool schema. Guarded by
``test_no_unexpected_openclaw_masked_tool_fields``; renaming this back turns
that test red rather than silently corrupting a card.

request_id.title: Request Id
request_id.description: Id of the approval record.
