link_expires_at.title: Link Expires At
link_expires_at.description: When the authorisation link itself stops working, as the vendor reported it. Composio varies the lifetime — 5 minutes and 10 have both been observed — so read it here rather than assuming one. Always earlier than ``deadline_at``, and it is not the deadline: a consent screen already open can still succeed after the link that opened it stops working, which is the ordinary case rather than an error. Use this only to stop offering the link again; keep counting down to ``deadline_at``.

ComposioConnectionDetail.title: ComposioConnectionDetail
ComposioConnectionDetail.description: The pollable state of one authorisation attempt.

redirect_url.title: Redirect Url
redirect_url.description: Composio-hosted authorisation URL to open. Treat as a credential for the life of the link — do not log it, store it, or share it outside the browser doing the authorising. Returned exactly once; polling will not repeat it.

ComposioConnectionStart.title: ComposioConnectionStart
ComposioConnectionStart.description:
The response to starting a flow: where to send the customer, and what to poll.

Both halves are needed and neither substitutes for the other. The redirect
is single-use and transient; ``connection`` is the durable handle that
survives the customer closing the popup, which is the case the whole flow
exists to make recoverable.

mcp_catalog_entry_id.title: Mcp Catalog Entry Id
mcp_catalog_entry_id.description: Catalog entry for the Composio tile being connected and installed

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description: Name for the MCP server this authorisation will install, unique per org. Omitted, blank, or whitespace falls back to the catalogue entry's own name, which is what a first install of a tile ordinarily wants. Supply it to install a second instance of a toolkit the org already has — a second Slack workspace, a sandbox alongside a production tile. Checked for availability when the flow starts, so a collision is reported while the field is still on screen rather than after the customer has authorised at the vendor.

mcp_connect_request_id.title: Mcp Connect Request Id
mcp_connect_request_id.description: The in-chat connect ask this attempt answers, if it came from a card. Binding it is what lets the ask be resumed after the browser goes away, and what tells the requesting bot its tile landed. Omit it for an install started from the MCP wizard, which has no ask behind it. Must name an ask in your own organization for the same catalogue entry.

ComposioConnectionStartRequest.title: ComposioConnectionStartRequest
ComposioConnectionStartRequest.description:
Everything a caller may say about an authorisation it is starting.

Three fields, and the asymmetry between them is the security property rather
than an inconsistency. ``mcp_catalog_entry_id`` is an id the platform wrote,
and the toolkit, the auth config name, the user id and above all the
**callback URL** are derived server-side from that entry and from deployment
settings. Composio does not validate callbacks, so any field here that could
reach one would be an open redirect carrying a fresh connected-account
handle.

``display_name`` reaches none of that. It is inert text, read exactly once —
at completion, as the name of the MCP server being created — and it is here
because the alternative was worse than the risk: deriving the name from the
catalogue entry meant every second install of a connect-first toolkit
collided on a name the operator never chose and could not change, so two
Slack workspaces were not expressible at all (#2632).

``mcp_connect_request_id`` is the third, and it is the one field here that is
a *reference to something the caller did not necessarily ask for*, so it is
checked rather than trusted. It says "this attempt answers that in-chat ask",
which is what makes the ask resumable and what decides — at settlement — which
bot is told the tile landed, in which conversation. An unchecked id would
therefore let any member who may install a tile aim a developer message at any
bot in the org, in a conversation they need not be able to read. The service
accepts it only when the ask is in the caller's own org and names the same
catalogue entry as the attempt; anything else is rejected rather than quietly
ignored, because silently dropping it would produce an attempt that settles
and tells nobody.

ComposioConnectionState.title: ComposioConnectionState
ComposioConnectionState.description:
Lifecycle of one connect-first install attempt.

Persisted as ``VARCHAR`` under a CHECK constraint rather than a native
PostgreSQL enum, for the same reason as
:class:`~botyard_core.models.database.botyard.org_composio_project.ComposioProjectStatus`:
adding a state stays a one-statement migration.

Named ``...State`` rather than ``...Status`` on purpose: the vendor's own
status vocabulary is
:class:`~botyard_core.services.composio.client.ComposioConnectionStatus`,
and the two are read side by side in the poll path. These are Botyard's own
reading of a connection, and the mapping between them is a decision
this service makes rather than a rename — notably ``UNKNOWN`` on the vendor
side maps to no terminal state here at all, only to "keep waiting until
``deadline_at``".

**Two axes, not one.** :attr:`is_terminal` asks whether the *install attempt*
is over; :attr:`is_installed` asks whether a tile exists. They were the same
question while ``connected`` was the only successful outcome, and
:attr:`NEEDS_REAUTH` is what separates them: the attempt finished, the tile
exists, and the connection is nonetheless not working. Read the one the call
site actually means — the install poll wants :attr:`is_terminal`, the CHECK
constraint and anything reasoning about the tile want :attr:`is_installed`.

name.title: Name
name.description: Wire key to submit this value under. Frequently a meaningless slot — ``builder_io`` calls its public key ``generic_api_key`` and its private key ``generic_id`` — so never infer sensitivity from it. Use ``is_secret``.

description.title: Description
description.description: The vendor's own help text for this field, if it ships one

is_secret.title: Is Secret
is_secret.description: Whether to mask this input: the vendor's own flag, OR'd with a password-name check. The vendor's flag alone is not reliable. It was right for every API_KEY toolkit checked, but four BASIC toolkits mark their required ``password`` as not secret. It governs **masking only**: every collected value is stored as a secret regardless, so a vendor flipping this flag can never silently downgrade a live credential.

required.title: Required
required.description: Whether the install is refused without it. About *presence*, not about being the credential — several toolkits require only a host or subdomain and make the key itself optional.

default.title: Default
default.description: The vendor's suggested value, to prefill the input with

ComposioCredentialFieldSpec.title: ComposioCredentialFieldSpec
ComposioCredentialFieldSpec.description:
One input a credential form must render, as the vendor describes it.

Public catalogue metadata throughout: a *description* of a credential, never
one. Nothing here is ever echoed back with a value in it, which is why this
shape has no ``value`` field even though it would be convenient for a form
that wants to round-trip its own state.

toolkit_slug.title: Toolkit Slug
toolkit_slug.description: Composio toolkit the fields belong to

fields.title: Fields
fields.description: In the vendor's order, required fields first

ComposioCredentialForm.title: ComposioCredentialForm
ComposioCredentialForm.description:
The fields to render for one API-key tile's install form.

Read live from the vendor on every request rather than from the catalogue,
which is the decision the whole flow rests on: Composio accepts field names
outside its own spec *silently* and answers 201 ``ACTIVE``, so a stored copy
that drifted would not fail on submit — it would store the customer's
credential under a key the vendor ignores and hand back a tile that looks
connected and cannot authenticate.

mcp_catalog_entry_id.title: Mcp Catalog Entry Id
mcp_catalog_entry_id.description: Catalog entry for the Composio tile being installed

values.title: Values
values.description: Vendor field name to value, as named by ``ComposioCredentialForm.fields``. Blank optional values are dropped rather than forwarded; an empty string is a value as far as the vendor is concerned.

vault_entry_refs.title: Vault Entry Refs
vault_entry_refs.description: Vendor field name to the ``entry_id`` of an existing Runtime Vault entry whose value should be used for that field, instead of typing it into ``values``. A field may appear in ``values`` or here, never both. Only entries the org itself owns resolve: a platform-managed credential, an entry of another organization, an expired entry or an unknown id are all refused with the same 422, so the answer never says which. Requires a signed-in person who may manage the org's vault policies (403 otherwise, including for bots and API keys). The value is **copied** at submit time: rotating the source entry later does not update the integration. Any field may be referenced, secret or not, because the vendor's ``is_secret`` flag is not trusted to decide how a value is handled.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description: Name for the MCP server this install creates, unique per org. Omitted, blank, or whitespace falls back to the catalogue entry's own name. Supply it to install a second instance of a toolkit the org already has against a different vendor account. Checked for availability before any vendor object or vault entry exists, so a collision costs the customer nothing to correct.

mcp_connect_request_id.title: Mcp Connect Request Id
mcp_connect_request_id.description: The in-chat connect ask this install answers, if it came from a card (platform-development #3014). Binding it is what lets a reopened card show the tile as installed, and what tells the requesting bot its tile landed. Omit it for an install started from the MCP wizard, which has no ask behind it. Must name an ask in your own organization for the same catalogue entry; anything else is refused with 404 before any vendor object or vault entry exists.

ComposioCredentialInstallRequest.title: ComposioCredentialInstallRequest
ComposioCredentialInstallRequest.description:
A submitted credential form.

``values`` is credential material. It is never logged, never echoed into an
error, and the vendor's own error body is withheld on this path for the same
reason — on the create endpoint that body can echo the request that produced
it. Everything the customer needs in order to correct a mistake is derived
from the *spec*, which is public.

Keys are checked against the live spec rather than trusted: an unknown name
is accepted silently by the vendor, so a submission carrying one is a
connection that cannot authenticate, reported as a success.

mcp_server_id.title: Mcp Server Id
mcp_server_id.description: The installed tile these credentials belong to

toolkit_slug.title: Toolkit Slug
toolkit_slug.description: Composio toolkit the fields belong to; NULL when this is not a Composio tile

fields.title: Fields
fields.description: In the vendor's order, required fields first, each carrying whether a value is stored. Empty when ``editable`` is false.

editable.title: Editable
editable.description: Whether this tile's credentials can be replaced from here. False for anything that is not a live Composio credential-form install — an OAuth tile, a plain remote server, a tile whose vendor objects are missing. Hide the section rather than rendering a form whose submit is going to be refused. Note that a tile with nothing stored is still editable: submitting every required field is how a tile installed before Botyard kept its own copy gets one.

vault_sync_state.description: Out-of-sync marker for a tile whose fields are linked to Runtime Vault secrets. NULL when the tile matches the vault (or links nothing).

vault_disconnect_reason.description: Why the tile was disconnected, when ``vault_sync_state`` is ``disconnected``; NULL otherwise. ``source_deleted``: a linked vault secret was deleted — the fields still carrying its ``source_vault_entry_id`` are the ones to re-point.

ComposioCredentialState.title: ComposioCredentialState
ComposioCredentialState.description:
What an installed tile's credential section renders.

A sibling of :class:`ComposioCredentialForm` rather than a subclass of it,
even though it reads as "the install form plus state". Narrowing an
inherited ``fields`` to a subclass of its element type is unsound as typing
— a ``ComposioCredentialForm`` reference could append a plain spec to it —
and buying that unsoundness with a ``type: ignore`` to save four lines is
not a trade this contract should make.

Returned for any MCP server the caller can see, including ones that have
nothing to do with Composio: the answer there is ``editable=False`` with no
fields, not a 404. A read that distinguishes "not a Composio tile" from "no
such server" by status code would make the Configuration tab branch on error
codes to decide whether to draw a section, and a 404 in a browser console is
a support question every time it is not a bug.

name.title: Name
name.description: Wire key to submit this value under. Frequently a meaningless slot — ``builder_io`` calls its public key ``generic_api_key`` and its private key ``generic_id`` — so never infer sensitivity from it. Use ``is_secret``.

description.title: Description
description.description: The vendor's own help text for this field, if it ships one

is_secret.title: Is Secret
is_secret.description: Whether to mask this input: the vendor's own flag, OR'd with a password-name check. The vendor's flag alone is not reliable. It was right for every API_KEY toolkit checked, but four BASIC toolkits mark their required ``password`` as not secret. It governs **masking only**: every collected value is stored as a secret regardless, so a vendor flipping this flag can never silently downgrade a live credential.

required.title: Required
required.description: Whether the install is refused without it. About *presence*, not about being the credential — several toolkits require only a host or subdomain and make the key itself optional.

default.title: Default
default.description: The vendor's suggested value, to prefill the input with

is_set.title: Is Set
is_set.description: Whether Botyard holds a stored value for this field. When ``value`` is null, render it as a 'set' indicator next to an **empty** input — never as a mask or a length. False on a field the customer has never filled in, and false for every field of a tile installed before Botyard kept its own copy.

source_vault_entry_id.title: Source Vault Entry Id
source_vault_entry_id.description: The Runtime Vault entry this field's stored value is linked to, when it was supplied as a vault reference rather than typed. The tile holds a linked copy: a change to that entry is pushed to the integration in the background (see ``vault_sync_state`` for a push that is pending, failed, or whose entry was deleted). NULL for a typed value.

value.title: Value
value.description: The stored value, **only** for a field that is plainly not a credential (a URL, a region, a subdomain): the vendor does not mark it secret, Botyard's catalogue snapshot does not either, and neither its name nor its label looks like a password, token, secret or key. Prefill the input with it; submitting it unchanged is the same as leaving the field alone. NULL for every secret field, for every field linked to a Runtime Vault entry (``source_vault_entry_id``), and for anything not stored. Only returned to callers who may replace this tile's credentials.

ComposioCredentialStateField.title: ComposioCredentialStateField
ComposioCredentialStateField.description:
One input on an *installed* tile's credential form.

The install form's field plus the one thing an edit form needs that an
install form does not: whether Botyard is already holding a value for it.
Deliberately an extension of :class:`ComposioCredentialFieldSpec` rather
than a parallel shape, because the fields themselves are the same live
vendor spec read the same way — an edit form that rendered a *stored* copy
of the spec would drift from the vendor exactly as an install form would.

For a credential, ``is_set`` is the only thing ever said about a stored
value. Not its length, not a masked prefix, not its age: a suffix or a
length is a real reduction of the search space for the value, and no part
of this screen needs one to do its job. The input beside it is empty, and
leaving it empty means "leave this one alone".

**The exception is a field that is plainly not a credential** (#3044), such
as a workspace URL, a region or a subdomain. Its stored value comes back in
``value`` so the form can show it prefilled and editable. The rule is in
:func:`botyard_core.services.composio.credential_display.may_display_stored_value`.
It needs the vendor's live flag, Botyard's catalogue snapshot and a broad
credential-name check to all agree. A field that is linked to a Runtime
Vault entry never carries a ``value``: that value belongs to the vault and
is shown under the vault's own permissions. ``value`` only ever reaches a
caller who may already replace this tile's credentials.

values.title: Values
values.description: Vendor field name to new value, as named by ``ComposioCredentialState.fields``. Send only the fields being changed: an omitted or blank field keeps its stored value. A submission with nothing non-blank in it is refused rather than treated as a no-op rotation, because rebuilding the connection is not free — it replaces the vendor account the tile's live session is pinned to.

vault_entry_refs.title: Vault Entry Refs
vault_entry_refs.description: Vendor field name to the ``entry_id`` of an existing Runtime Vault entry to use as that field's new value. Same rules as on install: a field may appear in ``values`` or here but not both, only org-owned entries resolve (anything else is the same 422), a signed-in person with vault-policy management is required, and the value is copied, not linked. A referenced field counts as changed.

ComposioCredentialUpdateRequest.title: ComposioCredentialUpdateRequest
ComposioCredentialUpdateRequest.description:
A submitted credential *edit*.

The same material, and the same handling rules, as
:class:`ComposioCredentialInstallRequest`: never logged, never echoed into
an error, and the vendor's own error body withheld because on this path it
can echo the request that produced it.

**Blank means "leave unchanged", and that is the only reading available.**
Composio has no in-place credential update — a ``PATCH`` of a connected
account returns ``200 {"success": true}`` and silently discards the
credential (probed 2026-09-18), and ``/refresh`` answers 409 telling the
caller to make a new connection — so every edit rebuilds the whole
connection from the whole field set, drawn from the vault for the fields the
customer left alone. A blank input therefore cannot mean "clear this field":
there is no request that clears one and keeps the rest, and inventing one
would mean submitting a connection the vendor would reject or, worse,
accept.

ComposioVaultDisconnectReason.title: ComposioVaultDisconnectReason
ComposioVaultDisconnectReason.description: Why a vault-linked tile was disconnected (#3016).

ComposioVaultSyncState.title: ComposioVaultSyncState
ComposioVaultSyncState.description:
Why a vault-linked tile may not match its Runtime Vault secrets right now (#3016).

Absent (``null``) means in sync: every linked field holds the vault's current value.

ConfigFieldDiff.title: ConfigFieldDiff
ConfigFieldDiff.description:
One differing field between ``desired_config`` and ``reconciled_config_json``.

``path`` is a dotted path rooted at a :data:`DIFFABLE_FIELDS` entry, e.g.
``"heartbeat.every"`` or ``"tools.allow"``. The first path segment
(``path.split(".")[0]``) is always one of :data:`DIFFABLE_FIELDS`, which
the frontend uses to route a diff entry to its owning card.

consent_shape.description: What authorising this tile hands over, as a closed classification: 'personal_identity' connects the approver's own account and carries their private surface; 'shared_account' connects an account the organisation controls; 'mailbox' hands over an entire mailbox; 'none' needs no disclosure; 'custom' means the operator wrote the disclosure themselves and it is in consent_note. Tell the approving human which of these applies before proposing the install

consent_title.title: Consent Title
consent_title.description: Headline of an operator-authored disclosure, present only when consent_shape is 'custom'. Read it together with consent_note: the two are one disclosure, and quoting the body to the approving human without the headline drops the part they would have read first

consent_note.title: Consent Note
consent_note.description: Tile-specific disclosure that must be shown to the human approving this install, when the tile carries one. Not a description: it is what the approver is agreeing to, not what the tile does. An addendum to consent_shape for the four canned shapes, never a replacement for one; when consent_shape is 'custom' this text is the body of the disclosure headed by consent_title, and is always present

packaging_kind.description: How the template itself is packaged (container_image, managed_remote or npx). Provenance only — do not pass it to create_mcp_server; pass runtime_kind.

requires_connect.title: Requires Connect
requires_connect.description: True when this tile is installed by *authorising* it, not by filling in a form. The create path refuses it: the server row is created only once a human has returned from the vendor's consent screen connected. Such a tile reads as zero-config — no configuration_fields, no credential_requirements — so without this flag the contract is indistinguishable from a one-call install that it is not.

configuration_fields.title: Configuration Fields
configuration_fields.description: Fields the install asks for: the template's form fields, or for a tile installed with the vendor's own credentials, the vendor's fields as snapshotted at import (target type vendor_credential; secret_ref-only fields are credentials, plaintext-only ones are not). Empty for such a tile when the snapshot was not captured

image.title: Image

port.title: Port
port.description: Container port this template pins. Locked unless ``configuration_fields`` exposes a top-level ``port`` target, so a configured create must pass exactly this value.

requires_credentials.title: Requires Credentials
requires_credentials.description: True when this tile is installed by a human entering the vendor's credentials into a Botyard form. The create path refuses it. When the vendor's field spec was captured at import, configuration_fields lists the fields (target type vendor_credential; secret_ref-only fields are credentials, plaintext-only ones are not) for display — the install still validates against the vendor's live spec. When it was not captured, configuration_fields is empty. An agent must not attempt to collect a credential itself; chat is not an acceptable channel for one.

ContainerImageMcpCatalogEntryDetail.description: The app's creation contract for a container-image (or npx) template.

name.title: Name
name.description: Human-readable label for the MCP server (unique per org)

slug.title: Slug
slug.description: URL-safe identifier — server-generated from ``name`` when omitted. Must match ``^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}$`` if provided.

description.title: Description
description.description: Optional free-form description shown alongside the server in the UI

mcp_catalog_entry_id.title: Mcp Catalog Entry Id
mcp_catalog_entry_id.description: Catalog entry used to prefill this create payload, if any

catalog_form_answers.title: Catalog Form Answers
catalog_form_answers.description: Answers to the linked template's setup form, keyed by form field id. The platform projects each answer onto the target the template declares for that field, so a caller never has to compile the form into env vars, mounts or headers itself — and never has to restate a value the template owns. Requires ``mcp_catalog_entry_id``; an unknown field id, a mode the field does not allow, or a missing required answer is refused by name. Answers are projected after template inheritance, so an answer always beats the template's baked default. tool_result_max_chars.title: Tool Result Max Chars
tool_result_max_chars.description: Ceiling for a single live tool result before truncation, in chars. Botyard pins OpenClaw's small-context default (16000, ~4k tokens) for every model instead of letting the >=200k-token auto cap (64000) apply, which is what lets a single 30-76 KB MCP response occupy the window. The value can only lower the effective cap — OpenClaw takes ``min(floor(contextWindow * 0.3) * 4, cap)`` — and truncation is explicit (a truncation notice is appended, minimum 2000 chars kept). None omits the key so OpenClaw uses its auto cap.

memory_get_max_chars.title: Memory Get Max Chars

memory_get_default_lines.title: Memory Get Default Lines

post_compaction_max_chars.title: Post Compaction Max Chars

ContextLimitsConfig.title: ContextLimitsConfig
ContextLimitsConfig.description:
Per-agent context budget ceilings serialized into the openclaw config.

The load-bearing knob is :attr:`tool_result_max_chars`. OpenClaw caps a
single *live* tool result at ``min(floor(contextWindow * 0.3) * 4, cap)``
chars (``resolveLiveToolResultMaxChars`` /
``calculateMaxToolResultCharsWithCap``), where ``cap`` is this config value
when set and otherwise an auto cap derived from the model's context window:
16k chars under 100k tokens, 32k at >=100k, **64k at >=200k**. Every Botyard
bot on a modern model therefore lands in the 64k bucket, so a single tool
result may legally consume ~16k tokens of context.

That auto cap is the mechanism behind the chronic context overflows: measured
botyard-mcp responses on a real bot (13-minute window, ~600 KB total) were
``search_conversation_history`` 76 KB, ``memory_search`` 36 KB, ``get_task``
31 KB, ``github_list_prs`` 31 KB, ``search_tasks`` 29 KB, ``list_my_tasks``
22 KB — i.e. all but one pass the 64k cap untouched, and a handful of them
fill the window. Sessions were observed overflowing at ~258k compaction
tokens with only 47-72 messages.

Unlike OpenClaw's cache-TTL context pruning (which Botyard switches off;
see the v2026.6.1 serializer) this does not depend on prompt-cache
eligibility — ``resolveAgentContextLimits`` takes no provider or auth input,
and the persistence write path is ungated (it even falls back to 16000
rather than "unbounded" when the context window is unknown). So on the
**embedded (pi) runner** it applies to every bot whatever model backs it.

Two scope limits worth knowing before relying on it:

* On **claude-cli** bots it does not bound the CLI's context at all. Claude
  Code's tool results never reach OpenClaw's persistence write path; the cap
  only feeds ``shouldPreemptivelyCompactBeforePrompt``'s size estimate.
* The mid-turn guard consumer reads it via ``midTurnPrecheckOptions``, so
  that particular path is live only because Botyard sets
  ``compaction.mid_turn_precheck=True``. The write-time cap itself is
  unconditional.

secret value.  The envelope carries the conversation/message context and the
primary ``resource_id`` carries the first redacted secret label/key path.

errors.title: Errors

wake_origin.title: Wake Origin
wake_origin.description: Why this row exists, when the bot was woken rather than written to: the process watch that resolved or the schedule that fired. Lets a client explain the resulting activity instead of showing an unexplained spinner. ``null`` for every ordinary message.

Distinct from ``created_at``, which for an assistant row is the moment the bot PICKED THE TURN UP — the row is created before any content so it can claim its ordinal — and therefore says nothing about how long the answer took. Clients should render elapsed time from ``completed_at`` when it is present, and the turn's duration as ``completed_at - created_at``. ``null`` means the turn is not known to have finished (still in flight, cancelled before it ran, or a row predating this field); fall back to ``created_at``.

from the user's open Bot Page, before it is shown to the bot. Page context

Such a time is real but it is the runtime's, not the process's: a pipe makes most programs block buffer, so a burst written over minutes can arrive at one instant and be stamped many times over with it. Consumers must present these as observed, never as a time the process itself claimed.

ConversationSource.title: ConversationSource
ConversationSource.description:
How a conversation entered the platform.

``web_chat`` is the default for app/chat-proxy origin (existing
behaviour). Email sources are retained for compatibility with historical
channel plans. Current Bot Email is captured by the Resend webhook in the
API; see ``docs/design/2026-07-27-email-service-boundaries.md``.

``scheduler`` marks a conversation auto-created to host an externalized
schedule's wakes (EPIC #493). These are automation threads, not
user-initiated chats, so conversation-listing surfaces hide them (see
``conversation_visibility_predicate``); the bot still reaches them
directly via the wake's ``conversation_id``.

``ms_teams`` marks conversations created by the Teams dispatcher on first
inbound contact.

``target_user_id`` the user it named (#3323), whose tab answered.

CreditsExhaustedMessageError.description:
The turn was refused because the LLM spend allowance is used up.

Split out of :class:`ProviderMessageError` because the provider's own words
are actively harmful here. OpenRouter answers a spent key with
``403 Key limit exceeded (total limit). Manage it using
https://openrouter.ai/workspaces/<workspace>/keys/<key-hash>`` — on a
Botyard-managed credential that URL and hash belong to *Botyard's*
OpenRouter workspace, not the customer's, so echoing it leaks our internal
key identity and points the user at a console they cannot open. It also
reads as a platform fault rather than "you are out of credits", which is
the one thing the user can actually act on.

So this error never carries the provider's message: ``message`` is composed
from ``managed`` at classification time and is safe to render verbatim.

An ORIGIN, not a full URL: the daemon appends the runtime route itself, so an operator cannot point a fleet at the wrong path. Returned on every exchange rather than configured on the device, so a hostname change reaches the fleet on its next assertion exchange — which is not the same as its next reconnect, because a live session handle is reused for its lifetime even across a dropped socket

DeviceAssertionExchangeResponse.title: DeviceAssertionExchangeResponse
DeviceAssertionExchangeResponse.description:
A short-lived session, bought by one assertion.

``session_token`` is returned exactly once and is never recoverable — only
its hash is stored.

*** THE TOKEN IS NOT A BEARER CAPABILITY AND ITS EXPIRY IS NOT THE
REVOCATION MECHANISM. *** Every use of it re-reads the device registry, so
a revoked device is denied on its next call whatever ``expires_at`` says.
``expires_at`` bounds how long a session may be reused; it says nothing
about how long a revoked device keeps working, which is "not at all".

``gateway_url`` is returned here rather than configured on the device. The
exchange is a live registry read, so sourcing the URL from it makes "holds
a gateway URL" imply "is a currently-valid device" — a stronger property
than enrollment can give, since enrollment only evidences a past event.

DeviceEnrollmentResponse.title: DeviceEnrollmentResponse
DeviceEnrollmentResponse.description:
A device this machine is, as of this call.

Carries only what the daemon needs to know which bot it now is. No
session, assertion or SVID is issued here — that belongs to the gateway,
and the device credential buys only the right to *ask* for one.

*** EVERY FIELD HERE CAME FROM THE DEVICE REGISTRY DURING THIS REQUEST.
*** That is the purpose of the response rather than a remark about it: an
installer may report success on what this call returned, and never on what
it found lying in ``~/.botyard``. A machine reading its own state file
cannot tell which bot that file belongs to *today*, nor whether the device
it names has since been revoked — and one that decided it could reported a
healthy install while holding revoked credentials for an unrelated bot.

This identifier is only automatically passed to the model when the `FileUrl` is returned by a tool.
If you're passing the `FileUrl` as a user message, it's up to you to include a separate text part with the identifier,
e.g. "This is file <identifier>:" preceding the `FileUrl`.

It's also included in inline-text delimiters for providers that require inlining text documents, so the model can
distinguish multiple files.

ExternalChatTenantPatch.title: ExternalChatTenantPatch
ExternalChatTenantPatch.description:
Change which bot answers, or unlink the tenant.

Omitted means unchanged, so a caller flipping ``is_active`` does not have to
restate the default bot and risk clearing it.

``UNSET`` rather than ``None`` as the "omitted" marker, because the two
fields disagree about what null means and collapsing them is a real bug:
null on ``default_bot_id`` legitimately clears the default, whereas null on
``is_active`` is meaningless and must not be coerced into ``False`` — that
would turn a malformed request into a silent unlink. Leaving ``None`` out of
``is_active``'s union makes that unrepresentable rather than merely
unlikely; an explicit null is a 422.

LlmChainEntry.title: LlmChainEntry
LlmChainEntry.description:
One credential link, in the bot's routing order — stored losslessly.

This is the **authoritative** record of a bot's LLM routing.
``primary``/``fallbacks``/``allowed_models``/``providers`` are derived from
it by :func:`derive_routing`; none of them is stored.

Why it has to live here rather than in ``bot_credential_links``: that table
is keyed ``(bot_id, scope, ordinal)`` and apply is a destructive
scope-replace, so ordinal — the very thing a reorder changes — is rewritten
and a removed entry's row simply vanishes. There is no stable per-entry
identity to hang a ``current_*`` column on, which is why credentials alone
can never answer "what was the chain before this change?". Storing the
chain in the config puts it on the same desired/reconciled footing as every
other stateful thing on the bot.

Why it can't be recovered from the derived fields either: an HTTP link
projects to ``ModelRef(provider="botyard", model=<id>)``, which carries no
credential identity, and :func:`derive_routing` collapses CLI entries that
share a ref, so the derived ref count is not the chain length. The
projection is lossy in that direction — which is exactly why the chain
itself must not be. One entry per eligible credential link, always; the
collapse happens at projection time and never in storage.

``routed_model`` is None for CLI-backed links — they are delivered through
``agents.defaults.cliBackends``, not ``models.providers``. Carrying the
resolved model here (rather than re-reading the credential preset) is what
keeps derivation a **pure, synchronous** function: the serializer has no
database session, so anything the wire format needs must already be in the
config.

MaintenancePolicyConfig.description:
Editable, persisted maintenance policy (per-org default).

Stored as JSONB on ``organizations.maintenance_policy`` (``None`` = no
configured policy, fall back to the hard-coded defaults). Distinct from
:class:`MaintenanceRestartPolicy`, which is the *resolved per-restart
snapshot* the engine consumes: :func:`resolve_restart_policy` turns this
config plus the restart's urgency into that snapshot.

``enabled=False`` opts the org out of workload-aware gating entirely —
regular restarts then apply immediately (today's blunt behaviour) instead
of waiting for idle/drain, while critical restarts are always immediate
regardless of this flag.

configured.title: Configured

MaintenanceRestartForceAppliedContent.title: MaintenanceRestartForceAppliedContent
MaintenanceRestartForceAppliedContent.description:
Typed content for an operator force-applying a pending maintenance restart.

Emitted when a platform admin invokes the "apply pending maintenance restart
now" fleet action, overriding the maintenance-window gate so a deferred /
parked restart lands immediately instead of waiting for the org's window.
``immediate`` records whether the operator chose to hard-kill this tick
(interrupting any active turn) versus a graceful drain; ``previous_phase`` is
the maintenance phase the restart was parked in before the override (e.g.
``deferred``); ``applied`` is whether the pod recreate landed within the
synchronous call (a graceful override on a still-busy bot may report ``False``
and finish draining on a later reconcile tick).

MaintenanceRestartMessageError.description:

ManagedRemoteOperation.title: ManagedRemoteOperation
ManagedRemoteOperation.description:
Why a managed-remote request is being made — recorded on every audit row.

Each member is bound to exactly one calling service identity by the API
(``READINESS`` → bot-provisioner; ``INVOKE`` and ``REFRESH`` →
botyard-mcp), so adding one never widens who may resolve credentials.

``INVOKE`` is a bot-initiated tool/resource/prompt call. ``REFRESH`` is
botyard-mcp's own background listing refresh, which no bot asked for; it
is a separate member so the secret-access audit trail can tell the two
apart (platform-development #3026).

McpCatalogEntryProvenance.title: McpCatalogEntryProvenance
McpCatalogEntryProvenance.description:
Which writer owns a catalog row's definition fields.

``source`` already answers *whose catalog a row appears in*; this answers
the different question of *who is allowed to overwrite it*. The two are not
the same, and conflating them is what breaks once more than one writer
exists: every ``botyard_builtin`` row used to come from
``mcp-catalog/manifest.yaml``, so "platform-owned" and "manifest-authored"
were interchangeable. With a vendor importer writing thousands of rows into
the same platform scope, they no longer are.

Each writer must confine itself to rows carrying its own provenance. The
manifest seeder must not touch a ``composio_toolkit`` row, and the importer
must not touch a ``manifest`` one — otherwise each run of either deletes or
resurrects the other's catalog, and the damage is silent because both
writers are idempotent against their own input and simply re-assert it.

Note what this does *not* govern: ``enabled`` is operator state, not
definition, and belongs to no writer here. See
:attr:`McpServerCatalogEntry.available` for that split.

How a *stored* form value should be interpreted.

McpCatalogPackagingKind.description:
How a catalog tile is packaged, which is not how its rows run.

Open-ended: a package-manager backed tile is a new label here and needs no
change to :class:`McpServerRuntimeKind`, because it still installs as one of
the runtimes that already exist. ``npx`` is the standing example — an npx
tile is deployed as a ``container_image`` row running the shared npx runner.

Shares the ``mcp_server_runtime_kind`` Postgres type with
:class:`McpServerRuntimeKind`; the labels are a superset, so the two map
onto the same type without a migration.

McpCatalogRecordColumn.description:
One typed column of a ``record_list`` field — a mini form field.

Columns are deliberately a smaller vocabulary than fields: no
``integration`` (a connection is a server-level decision, not a row's),
no ``password`` (``secret_ref`` is the vault-backed way to ask), no
``textarea`` (a table cell), and no nested ``record_list``.

id.title: Id

description.description: Help text shown as the column header's tooltip

required.title: Required

unique.title: Unique

pattern.description: Python/JavaScript-compatible regular expression a plaintext cell must fully match (text and text_or_secret_ref columns only)
pattern.title: Pattern

pattern_message.description: Message shown when a cell does not match pattern
pattern_message.title: Pattern Message

default_value.description: Value a newly added row starts with. Never allowed on secret-capable columns: a template does not answer a credential question.
default_value.title: Default Value

options.description: Allowed option values for select columns
options.title: Options

display.description: Optional widget hint, with the same rules as a field's display: select columns accept dropdown/radio/segmented, boolean columns switch/checkbox.
display.title: Display

suggested_secret_path.title: Suggested Secret Path

width.title: Width

advanced.title: Advanced

McpCatalogRecordListCompile.description:
How a ``record_list`` answer compiles into the field's env target as JSON.

The JSON lands in ``env_plaintext[target.name]``. A secret cell never does:
it becomes its own generated ``env_secret_refs`` entry named
``<secret_env_prefix>_<row>``, and the JSON carries only
``secret_placeholder % name`` (``${NAME}`` by default) for an env-expanding
consumer to resolve. Generated names are positional — reordering rows
renames them — so they are never an identity, only a slot.

shape.description: object: keyed by key_column; array: a list of row values
shape.title: Shape

key_column.description: Column whose (required, unique) cell keys each row; object shape only
key_column.title: Key Column

value.description: What each row becomes. Required for object shape; for array shape it defaults to an object of every column keyed by column id.

secret_placeholder.description: How a secret cell appears inside the JSON; %s is the generated env name
secret_placeholder.title: Secret Placeholder

secret_env_prefix.description: Prefix for generated secret env vars: <prefix>_<row>
secret_env_prefix.title: Secret Env Prefix

column.title: Column

One column placed into a row's output object, at an optional dotted path.

The field is ``path``, not ``key``: OpenClaw's transcript redactor masks any
property named ``key``, which would corrupt the tile in the bot's own view.

column.description: Column id whose cell is placed here
column.title: Column

path.title: Path

McpCatalogVendorAuthMode.title: McpCatalogVendorAuthMode
McpCatalogVendorAuthMode.description:
How an end user proves identity to the vendor behind a catalog entry.

Coarse on purpose. Vendors describe dozens of auth schemes and Composio
alone advertises nine across its toolkits; what the product needs is not a
faithful transcription of the vendor's taxonomy but the small number of
distinctions that change what we show a customer and whether the tile can
work at all.

The load-bearing one is ``OAUTH2_UNMANAGED``. A toolkit can advertise OAuth2
and still have no Botyard-registered OAuth client behind it, which looks
identical to ``OAUTH2_MANAGED`` right up to the point where the customer
clicks connect and the flow dies. Roughly 87 Composio toolkits are in that
state. Recording the distinction is what lets us seed them without shipping
a tile that installs cleanly and then cannot authorise.

``OTHER`` is the catch-all and exists so an unrecognised vendor scheme
downgrades a single tile's disclosure rather than failing an import of
thousands. A row that lands here is seeded disabled.

value.title: Value
value.description: The plaintext answer; set only for mode plaintext

secret_ref.description: The proposed vault secret; set only for mode secret_ref

McpConnectPrefillAnswer.title: McpConnectPrefillAnswer
McpConnectPrefillAnswer.description:
One answer the bot prefilled on a ``FORM`` connect card.

Exactly one of ``value`` (``plaintext``) or ``secret_ref`` (``secret_ref``)
is set. A plaintext answer is never a secret: the tool refuses plaintext for
any field that accepts a vault reference at all, and never takes a
``password`` field, so nothing stored here is credential material.

key_path.title: Key Path
key_path.description: Runtime Vault key path the bot named

vault_entry_id.title: Vault Entry Id
vault_entry_id.description: The org-owned vault entry that key path resolved to. What the credential install takes in vault_entry_refs.

display_name.title: Display Name
display_name.description: The entry's display name, for the card's chip

McpConnectPrefillSecretRef.title: McpConnectPrefillSecretRef
McpConnectPrefillSecretRef.description:
A vault secret the bot proposed for a secret field, resolved server-side.

The bot names it by key path; ``request_mcp_connection`` resolves the path
through the bot's own lease predicate when the ask is recorded, so a bot can
only ever propose a secret it could lease itself, and the card never has to
resolve a path (platform-development #3014). Identity and label only — the
value never leaves the vault on this path.

request_id.title: Request Id
request_id.description: The ask this state belongs to

mcp_catalog_entry_id.title: Mcp Catalog Entry Id
mcp_catalog_entry_id.description: Catalogue tile the ask would authorise

variant.description: Which card the ask renders as; see McpConnectRequest.variant

prefill.title: Prefill
prefill.description: Answers the bot prefilled for a form card, in field order. Plaintext answers are never secrets; secret answers are vault references already resolved to the entry and checked against the bot's own lease access. Editable by the human before they submit.

connection.description: The attempt this ask resolves to, or NULL if nobody has pressed connect yet — which is the ordinary state of a card nobody has acted on, not an error. A ``pending`` attempt here is one to resume polling, including the case where the browser that started it is long gone.

McpConnectRequestState.title: McpConnectRequestState
McpConnectRequestState.description:
What became of one in-chat connect ask, as the card reads it on mount.

Deliberately *not* a status of its own. The ask row stores no lifecycle —
``ComposioConnectService.get_status`` is the sole compare-and-set authority
over an authorisation, and a second stored status would be a second authority
for the same fact — so this is the ask plus at most one attempt, and the card
derives what to draw from the attempt's own state.

One ask can have produced several attempts (the duplicate-name check answers
409 with the name field still on screen, so rename-and-retry is ordinary), so
``connection`` is the *resolved* one: the authorisation that succeeded if any
did, else the one still in flight, else the most recent to have ended. Which
is to say: the answer to "is there anything here for the reader to know or to
resume", never a list for a client to choose from.

``redirect_url`` is absent, as it is from every read. Resuming an attempt
means resuming its **poll**, not recovering its link.

McpConnectVariant.description:
Which in-chat card a ``request_mcp_connection`` ask renders as.

Derived by the server from the catalogue tile when the ask is recorded,
never chosen by the bot (platform-development #3014):

* ``CONNECT`` — a connect-first tile: the human authorises at the vendor.
* ``FORM`` — a tile with fields to fill in: the vendor's credential form, or
  a template's configuration form. Answers the bot prefilled ride along.
* ``CONFIRM`` — a zero-configuration tile: the human only confirms.
McpConnectVariant.title: McpConnectVariant

McpConsentShape.description:
What a customer is actually agreeing to when they authorise a tile.

For the four *canned* members the member selects the disclosure and the
*copy* belongs to the frontend. That split is most of the point of the type:
an operator picking a member cannot mistype a claim about the customer's
data, and an operator who has never seen this file is not silently asked to
compose one.

Before this existed the App shipped one hardcoded paragraph above every
Authorise button, asserting all three of *connects as you*, *shared
org-wide*, and *carries your private surface*. That is true of Slack and
false of Google Ads, where the account being linked belongs to the company,
not to the person clicking. A disclosure that overstates is not harmless: it
trains people to skip the next one.

``SHARED_ACCOUNT`` and ``NONE`` both drop the personal-surface claim, and
they are not the same. ``SHARED_ACCOUNT`` still has an authorisation step
and still shares one credential across every bot in the org — the customer
needs to know that — whereas ``NONE`` is a tile with nothing to disclose at
all. Collapsing them would put a tile with real org-wide reach behind
silence.

:attr:`NONE` is deliberately explicit rather than modelled as an absent
value. The column is NOT NULL precisely so that "no warning" is something an
operator chose and can be seen to have chosen, instead of the state a row
falls into when nobody got round to classifying it.

**Why :attr:`CUSTOM` exists, and why it is not the exception that eats the
rule.** A closed enum is correct when the platform owns the claim. The rule
it was borrowed from guards a statement about *Botyard's own* data handling
("your prompts are never used for training"), which an operator must not be
able to forge or soften. This disclosure is a different sentence: it
describes what a *third-party* OAuth tile hands over, which is precisely the
thing the operator knows and the platform does not. There is no platform
claim to impersonate here — the operator is the accountable author of the
true statement, and four canned members can only ever approximate it. The
"admin" in question is Botyard staff in Admin -> MCP catalogue; the threat
model is an honest typo, not a hostile tenant.

The cost is real and was accepted deliberately rather than argued away: a
*stale* custom disclosure is worse than a generic-but-true one, because
specificity reads as authority. The mitigations are an audit trail that
keeps both sides of every edit (see
:class:`~botyard_core.audit_events.AdminMcpCatalogEntryUpdatedContent`) and
deliberate selection, not prohibition.

``CUSTOM`` is the one member whose *note* is load-bearing: it replaces the
platform paragraph rather than sitting beneath it, so a ``CUSTOM`` row with
no note is a shape naming a text that does not exist — an empty warning box
at the Authorise click. That state is refused by the API and by
``ck_mcp_catalog_custom_shape_requires_consent_note``, and unlike
``operator_consent_note_required`` the requirement is intrinsic to the
member rather than a separate flag an operator sets.
McpConsentShape.title: McpConsentShape

McpCredentialDestinationAcknowledgedCont.title: McpCredentialDestinationAcknowledgedContent
McpCredentialDestinationAcknowledgedCont.description:
Typed content for accepting a new destination for an org's secrets.

A managed-remote MCP row with Runtime Vault-backed ``secret_headers`` has
its secrets resolved server-side into every outbound request, so whoever
owns ``endpoint_url`` owns where they land. Nominating that host is
permitted — the operator is the org owner, and the vault is theirs — but
it is not permitted *quietly*, which is what this event is for.

``acknowledged_host`` is what the caller explicitly accepted, recorded
separately from ``new_host`` even though the service refuses unless they
match: the record should show the acceptance as the caller expressed it,
not merely the outcome the server derived.

``secret_key_paths`` are vault *references*, never values — the same
strings already stored on the row. The values are resolved at dial time
and appear nowhere in the database, the logs, or here.

attempted_at.title: Attempted At
attempted_at.description: When the handshake attempt was made (UTC)

outcome.description: Whether the attempt succeeded or failed

failure_kind.description: Classification of the failure; null on a successful attempt

error.title: Error
error.description: Diagnostic message for a failed attempt — the underlying handshake error plus the remedy, identical to the ``last_error`` this attempt produced. Never contains a credential value.

tool_count.title: Tool Count
tool_count.description: Tools returned by a successful attempt; null on a failed attempt

McpHandshakeAttempt.title: McpHandshakeAttempt
McpHandshakeAttempt.description:
One recorded ``tools/list`` handshake attempt against an MCP server.

The reconciler appends one of these per attempt — success or failure —
so a server's owner can diagnose a broken server through ordinary
org-scoped tooling instead of needing cluster log access. Attempts are
org-scoped implicitly: they live on the ``provider_mcp_servers`` row and
are only ever read through org-filtered queries.

**This model must never carry a credential.** ``extra="forbid"`` plus the
absence of any value-bearing field is the mechanical guard: the failure
path records key *paths* and header *names* (the pointers already exposed
on the server detail) and the exception text, never a resolved header
value. The provisioner cannot leak one by accident either — managed-remote
headers are resolved inside the outbound httpx auth flow, so the phase
that writes this record never holds the plaintext.

McpHandshakeFailureKind.title: McpHandshakeFailureKind
McpHandshakeFailureKind.description:
Classification of a ``tools/list`` handshake failure.

Lives here (rather than beside the reconciler that produces it) because
the value is persisted on ``provider_mcp_servers.handshake_attempts`` and
projected into the org-facing API/MCP contracts — model layers must be
able to name the type without importing the provisioner service package.
:mod:`botyard_core.services.provisioner.mcp_handshake` re-exports it for
the reconciler's own call sites.

The reconciler maps this + the server's ``runtime_kind`` /
``pod_host_mode`` into a ``last_error`` that tells the server's owner
(who only sees ``get_mcp_server``) exactly which knob to turn.

McpHandshakeOutcome.title: McpHandshakeOutcome
McpHandshakeOutcome.description: Whether a recorded ``tools/list`` handshake attempt worked.

McpImagePushApprovalDetails.title: McpImagePushApprovalDetails
McpImagePushApprovalDetails.description: ``mcp_image.push`` carries nothing structured beyond its spec's lines.

McpPodHostMode.title: McpPodHostMode
McpPodHostMode.description:
How Botyard sets the HTTP ``Host`` when connecting to an in-cluster MCP pod.

This is a fixed property of the server's HTTP framework, declared as
configuration (like ``port``) rather than discovered at runtime:

* ``natural`` — send the pod's in-cluster Service FQDN as ``Host`` (httpx's
  default). Correct for the MCP Python SDK / uvx, Node/npx, and every
  first-party ``ghcr.io/botyard-ai/*`` wrapper image. The default.
* ``pod_localhost`` — send ``Host: localhost:<port>``. Required by servers
  that enforce DNS-rebinding host allowlists (``mark3labs/mcp-go``, e.g.
  ``grafana/mcp-grafana``), which reject the Service FQDN with
  ``403 forbidden: host not allowed``. Sending it to a server that does not
  want it (Python SDK) instead breaks the handshake with ``Session
  terminated`` (the server's ``307`` echoes the forged Host back to the
  client's own localhost).

Only meaningful for ``runtime_kind=container_image``; ignored for
``managed_remote`` (the vendor host is always preserved).

McpServerAccess.title: McpServerAccess
McpServerAccess.description:
MCP server reachability within its organization.

The one-for-one mirror of :class:`BotAccess`, and deliberately so — epic
#2672 D10 chose to reproduce the bot access mode rather than invent a
narrower one, because the alternative (an ambient term discriminated by
actor type, "all bots but no humans") would have been a new capability in
the shared policy engine rather than a column on this table.

``OPEN`` therefore means **fully** open: the listing rule's ambient term
admits every principal the base permission admits, and ``mcp_server.read``
is held by ``org:member`` *and* ``org:viewer`` and by API-key actors. It is
not "every bot in the org"; it is everyone. The ``restricted`` default
exists so that is only ever true because somebody chose it.

access.description: Org-level reachability. 'restricted' means only this server's members reach it. 'open' means every principal in the organization holding mcp_server.read does — every member and viewer, every bot, and every API key.

McpServerAccessUpdate.title: McpServerAccessUpdate
McpServerAccessUpdate.description:
Request to set an MCP server's org-level access mode (epic #2672 D10).

A body of one required field, on a route of its own, rather than a field on
``McpServerUpdate``. The separation is the authorization statement: ``PATCH``
is gated on org-wide ``mcp_server.update``, and who reaches a server is a
per-instance question that an instance owner — who may be a plain
``org:member`` — must be able to answer for their own server. Folding the
mode into the patch body would have made the narrower authority documented
and the wider one effective.

``access`` is required, with no default. On a route whose entire purpose is
to set one value, a default would let an empty body silently mean
``restricted``: a request that reads as "leave it alone" and closes the
server instead.

total_count.title: Total Count
total_count.description: Live tools this server currently exposes

bots.title: Bots
bots.description: Every bot in the org, assigned or not, ordered by name

McpServerAssignments.title: McpServerAssignments
McpServerAssignments.description:
Per-bot coverage of one MCP server's tools, for every bot in the org.

``total_count`` is the denominator every row shares — the number of live
tools this server currently exposes — so the caller renders "n of m"
without a second read, and bots holding nothing are still listed (that is
how you grant to a bot that has never used this server).

assigned_count.title: Assigned Count
assigned_count.description: How many of this server's live tools the bot currently holds

sync_status.description: Worst-case async config-apply status across this bot's assignments from this server (failed > pending > synced), or null when it holds none. Worst-case rather than an aggregate so a single stuck row stays visible.

McpServerBotAssignment.title: McpServerBotAssignment
McpServerBotAssignment.description:
One org bot's coverage of a single MCP server's tools.

The read behind the server page's Assignments tab, which is **bot-first**:
the bot is the subject and the server's tools are the object ("this bot
holds 12 of Outlook's 42 tools"), rather than fanning one tool out across
bots. Writes still go through the per-bot assignment endpoints — this model
is a projection, never an authorization decision.

``assigned_count`` counts only live tool rows (``deleted_at IS NULL``), so a
bot still holding a retired row from a deleted-and-recreated server is not
credited with coverage it does not have. Those orphans are invisible here by
construction: their ``mcp_server_id`` was nulled by the delete.

org_id.title: Org Id
org_id.description: Owning org for custom templates; null for Botyard built-ins

name.title: Name
name.description: Human-readable label; the operator's override when one is set

description.title: Description
description.description: Optional summary; the operator's override when one is set

logo_url.title: Logo Url
logo_url.description: The logo URL to display: the operator's override when one is set, otherwise the vendor's own as imported. Provenance only when no override exists — prefer logo_href in that case, which is same-origin

logo_href.title: Logo Href
logo_href.description: Same-origin URL to render this entry's logo from, or null when no artwork is cached. Prefer this over logo_url for display: the logo is painted through a CSS mask, which is a CORS-restricted resource, so a third-party URL that sends no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header paints nothing at all. Suppressed when the operator has overridden the logo, so that the override wins over the cached copy of the artwork it replaced

consent_shape.description: Which disclosure to render at this tile's authorisation step. For the four canned members the client owns the copy and must not derive it from any other field; a client that does not recognise a member shows its strongest disclosure rather than none. 'custom' is the exception: the operator authored the disclosure and it arrives in consent_title plus consent_note, which the client renders in place of its own title and paragraphs

consent_title.title: Consent Title
consent_title.description: Headline of an operator-authored disclosure. Non-null only when consent_shape is 'custom', where it is always present and renders in the same bold slot the client uses for its own disclosure titles. Null for every other shape: their titles are client-owned copy, and an addendum carrying its own headline would outrank the disclosure it sits beneath

consent_note.title: Consent Note
consent_note.description: Tile-specific disclosure text to show at the authorisation step. Null for most tiles. For the four canned shapes this is an addendum to consent_shape and never a replacement for it; when consent_shape is 'custom' it is the BODY of the disclosure, beneath consent_title, and is always present

packaging_kind.description: How this tile is packaged. Not what its rows run as — translate with server_runtime_kind_for_packaging()

env_secret_refs.title: Env Secret Refs
env_secret_refs.description: Env-var name to secret key path references

secret_file_mounts.title: Secret File Mounts
secret_file_mounts.description: Container file path to secret key path references

form_spec_version.title: Form Spec Version
form_spec_version.description: Dynamic form spec version, null when no template form is configured

form_spec.description: Optional dynamic setup form rendered for this catalog entry

requires_connect.title: Requires Connect
requires_connect.description: Whether installing this tile is an authorisation rather than a form. True means the customer is sent to the vendor to approve access and the server is created only once they return connected, so a client must offer the authorisation step instead of the configuration form: the tile has no fields to fill in, and the ordinary create path refuses it.

requires_credentials.title: Requires Credentials
requires_credentials.description: Whether installing this tile means collecting the vendor's credentials in a Botyard form. Mutually exclusive with requires_connect: a client offers the credential form when this is true, the authorisation step when requires_connect is true, and the ordinary configuration form when neither is. The fields to render are not in this payload and must be fetched per-tile, because they come from the vendor and are read live rather than stored.

connect_auth_mode.description: How this tile is installed, or null when it needs neither flow. Branch on this only for *copy*, never to decide which flow applies: requires_connect and requires_credentials already answer that, and this field is null unless one of them is true. 'oauth2_managed' means the customer signs in to the vendor; 'api_key', 'basic' and 'bearer_token' all mean they enter credentials into a Botyard form that stores them, and must be treated alike — despite the name, some 'api_key' toolkits ask for a username and password, so copy should say 'credentials' rather than 'API key'. A client that does not recognise the value should fall back to the neutral wording rather than assume a sign-in.

enabled.title: Enabled
enabled.description: Whether this entry appears in setup flows

created_at.title: Created At
created_at.description: When the catalog entry was created

McpServerCatalogEntry.title: McpServerCatalogEntry
McpServerCatalogEntry.description:
Reusable MCP setup catalog entry.

``name``, ``description`` and ``logo_url`` carry the **resolved** copy: the
operator's override when one is set, the vendor's text otherwise. The
resolution happens here, at validation, rather than at each call site —
``validation_alias`` points the fields at the ORM row's ``display_*``
hybrids, so every reader that builds this model ``from_attributes`` gets the
override whether or not it knew the override existed.

``consent_note`` resolves the same way but has no vendor fallback: it is
operator-authored or absent. It is a separate field from ``description``
rather than a longer description because the two are read at different
moments — the description while browsing, the note at the click of
Authorise — and because a consent string sharing a slot with browsing copy
can be deleted by an edit nobody reviews as a safety change.

That indirection is the point. The operator-owned columns exist so Botyard
can put its own words on a tile — for Slack, a consent disclosure saying the
connection authorises as the approving human. A projection that read the
vendor columns directly would drop that text without failing anything, which
is the exact shape of the ``tool_scope`` bug in platform-development #2497:
an override nobody reads.

``populate_by_name`` keeps ``McpServerCatalogEntry(name=...)`` working for
the callers that build this model from a dict rather than an ORM row.

McpServerCreateApprovalDetails.title: McpServerCreateApprovalDetails
McpServerCreateApprovalDetails.description: ``mcp_server.create`` carries nothing structured beyond its spec's lines.

McpServerDesiredState.title: McpServerDesiredState
McpServerDesiredState.description: Control-plane intent for an MCP server.

McpServerHealth.title: McpServerHealth
McpServerHealth.description:
One org MCP server's health as an account picker shows it (bot catalogue P3).

Read from stored state only, never from a vendor call: see
:func:`botyard_core.services.api.mcp_server_health.server_health` for the
rule. Three values, because a picker has three things to say: use it, fix
the sign-in, or expect it not to work.

actor_type.description: Kind of principal: user, bot or api_key

actor_id.title: Actor Id
actor_id.description: ID of the member principal, in its own table's namespace

role.title: Role
role.description: Capacity the principal is attached in, e.g. 'owner', 'member'

name.title: Name
name.description: Display name of the principal; null when it no longer exists

avatar_url.title: Avatar Url
avatar_url.description: Avatar for user and bot members; always null for API keys

McpServerMember.title: McpServerMember
McpServerMember.description:
One principal on an MCP server's member list, with display fields resolved.

The membership row itself is polymorphic on both axes and carries no
foreign key to any principal table, so ``name`` and ``avatar_url`` are
resolved alongside it rather than joined — see
``botyard_core.services.api.resource_members.resolve_member_identities``.
Both are optional because a membership row outlives the principal it names:
``actor_id`` has no referential integrity, so a deleted bot leaves a row
that an owner still needs to see in order to remove it.

``role`` is a plain string, not an enum. The vocabulary is per resource type
and grows a runtime half when customer-defined roles arrive
(``botyard_core.authz.membership``); freezing it into the wire contract here
would put a client-side migration in front of every new role.

actor_type.description: Kind of principal to add. Must be one the server's membership relation admits (user, bot or api_key); anything else is refused rather than stored as a row that grants nothing.

actor_id.title: Actor Id
actor_id.description: ID of the principal, in its own table's namespace

role.title: Role
role.description: Capacity to attach the principal in. 'member' reaches the server; 'owner' additionally edits this list. Defaults to the lesser of the two.

McpServerMemberAdd.title: McpServerMemberAdd
McpServerMemberAdd.description:
Request to put a principal on an MCP server's member list, or change its role.

Add-or-update, so the body is the *desired* state of one membership rather
than a request to create one: sending it twice is not an error, which is what
makes "an owner re-adds the person who was stranded" a safe instruction
rather than one that fails the second time somebody tries it.

``actor_type`` is explicit rather than inferred from the id. Ids are UUIDs
drawn from three different tables and nothing about their shape says which,
so inference would be a guess that silently writes a row matching nobody —
the exact accepted-and-inert failure this endpoint validates against.

McpServerRuntimeKind.title: McpServerRuntimeKind
McpServerRuntimeKind.description:
How an org-scoped MCP server row actually runs.

Deliberately closed. Every member here is a shape a ``provider_mcp_servers``
row can hold and a create body can name, and every create/update model pins
one of them as a ``Literal`` discriminator. A value that cannot appear on a
row does not belong in this enum: it used to carry ``npx``, which no row has
ever held and no create model would accept, and advertising it to agents as
a runtime kind produced calls the tool could only refuse (PlatDev #2475).

How a *catalog tile* is packaged is a separate vocabulary —
:class:`McpCatalogPackagingKind` — related to this one by exactly one public
translation, :func:`server_runtime_kind_for_packaging`.

McpServerSetupSource.title: McpServerSetupSource
McpServerSetupSource.description: How an MCP server row was created in the setup flow.

McpServerState.title: McpServerState

Observed lifecycle state of an org-scoped MCP server pod.

Mirrors the bot reconciler phase pipeline: a discrete ``pending`` /
``failed`` / ``stopped`` / ``deleting`` plus ``provisioning:*`` /
``awaiting_ready`` / ``running`` progression.

Send a block to set resources on top of the server's current shape; send null to reset to the platform default shape; omit to leave unchanged. Billed like bot resources and capped by the plan's per-MCP-server maximums. Changing it restarts the pod. Container-image rows only.

catalog_form_answers.title: Catalog Form Answers
catalog_form_answers.description: Re-answer this server's ``record_list`` template fields, keyed by field id, as ``{items: [{column: {mode, value}}]}``. The server compiles each list onto the env target JSON and its positional vault-backed slots, replacing whatever the field wrote before; a ``secret_ref`` cell's value is a Runtime Vault key path. Other field kinds are edited through the env maps they compile to. Container-image rows created from a template only.

acknowledged_credential_host.title: Acknowledged Credential Host
acknowledged_credential_host.description: Destination the caller accepts will receive this server's Runtime Vault secrets. Required when re-pointing ``endpoint_url`` at a different authority on a managed-remote row that has ``secret_headers``; must equal the authority of the new ``endpoint_url`` — its host, plus ``:port`` when the port is not the scheme default. Changing only the path on the same authority needs nothing — the secret already goes there; changing the port does need it, because a different port can be a separately operated listener. Naming the destination rather than sending a bare flag is deliberate: it proves the caller knew *where* the secret was going, and a destination changed after the confirmation was shown no longer matches. Recorded to the audit trail.

request_timeout_seconds.title: Request Timeout Seconds
request_timeout_seconds.description: Per-server gateway request-timeout override (seconds). Send an explicit null to clear it and inherit the gateway default. Applies to both runtime kinds.

McpServerUpdate.title: McpServerUpdate
McpServerUpdate.description:
Request to update mutable fields on an existing MCP server.

Stays flat (no discriminated union) because PATCH bodies arrive without
the client necessarily knowing the row's runtime_kind. The service
layer enforces per-runtime-kind shape after loading the row:
container_image rows reject ``endpoint_url``, managed_remote rows
reject every container-only field.

``runtime_kind`` and ``transport`` are intentionally absent — changing
either requires delete-and-recreate so the reconciler doesn't need to
re-plan pod primitives mid-flight.

MeterAggregation.title: MeterAggregation
MeterAggregation.description:
Supported meter aggregation functions.

Mirrors the Polar SDK ``Func`` enum — keep in sync. Polar does not
support ``COUNT`` as a meter aggregation (use ``SUM`` over a constant
value instead).

quantity.title: Quantity
quantity.description: Aggregated meter value for the bucket (the *gross* total — for overage meters this is the whole reservation, included + overage)

included.title: Included
included.description: Portion of ``quantity`` within the included baseline, when the series carries a per-bucket split (resource-overage meters). The overage portion is ``quantity - included``. Null for count meters, whose included threshold is a flat plan scalar (``OrgUsageMeter.included_units``) the client applies as a cap instead.

MeterHistoryPoint.title: MeterHistoryPoint
MeterHistoryPoint.description: One bucket in a meter history series.

total.title: Total
total.description: Aggregate quantity across all buckets in the window

MeterHistorySeries.title: MeterHistorySeries
MeterHistorySeries.description:
Per-meter usage history returned by ``GET /v1/orgs/{org_id}/usage/history``.

``points`` is empty when the meter has no events for the org in the
requested window — a fresh org or a brand-new meter both render as
a flat-zero chart without any special-casing on the FE.

MeterInfo.title: MeterInfo
MeterInfo.description: A meter definition from the billing provider.

MeterKey.title: MeterKey
MeterKey.description:
Registry meter slugs — every countable unit a plan can gate on.

All meters are metered (Polar ``metered_unit`` + optional
``meter_credit`` benefit for included units). An entry here means the
slug is recognized by the codebase; an entry in
``scripts/billing/registry.py::METER_DEFINITIONS`` wires it to the
provider.

The ``*_COUNT`` meters are AVG-over-daily-snapshots counts (bots, seats,
MCP servers). The ``*_OVERAGE`` meters bill the same way — AVG over daily
snapshots — but of the day's time-average net resource-overage from the
allocation ledger (vCore for CPU, GiB for memory/storage), priced at an
integer €/unit-month rate (the "GB-Month" convention, calendar-independent).
Each meters one billable :class:`MeteredResource` line-item independently —
the included baseline is subtracted per-interval in the collector, so the
snapshot carries net overage (Polar prices the averaged units; no
meter-credit benefit). ``memory_request`` and ``gpu`` are recorded in the
ledger but not metered to the provider yet.

MeteredResource.title: MeteredResource
MeteredResource.description:
A billable resource line-item the allocation ledger meters independently.

The ledger is long: one interval row per ``(consumer, metered_resource)``.
CPU and memory split into a reserved floor (``*_request``) and a burstable
ceiling (``*_limit``) because they are priced on both dimensions; storage and
gpu are single-dimension (fully reserved). New line-items are added by
extending this enum + a one-time migration — never by widening the table.

ModelCatalogueProposalStatus.description:
Where a catalogue proposal is in its lifecycle (PlatDev #3805).

``PENDING`` is the only open state. The other three are terminal:
``APPROVED`` and ``REJECTED`` record an admin's decision, and
``SUPERSEDED`` means upstream moved again before anyone decided.

Powers the admin model-editor's live prefill. ``owns_native_compaction`` is
true when the API's backend manages compaction itself (Codex harness), in
which case the knobs are inert and the editor shows a "not used" note.

``chain`` is authoritative. ``primary``, ``fallbacks``, ``allowed_models``
and ``providers`` are **not stored** — read them through
:func:`derive_routing`, or via the convenience properties below.

ModelDataRights.description:
What the provider may do with traffic sent to a model.

Deliberately a small, honest vocabulary rather than a marketing one. It is
left NULL for any model whose terms we have not actually checked: an
unverified "private" is a claim about a customer's data that we would have
invented, and that is worse than saying nothing.

Wider than :class:`InputModality` (the OpenClaw-facing preset column): the
catalogue records PDF documents, audio and video too, so a media gate can
ask "does this model read a PDF" (PlatDev #3072). A value outside this set
fails the models.dev boundary rather than being dropped.

A reference to a model within an OpenClaw provider.

and model is the model ID within that provider (e.g. ``"gpt-5.4"``).

MyPermissionsResponse.title: MyPermissionsResponse
MyPermissionsResponse.description:
What the caller may do in this org, as a lookup table for rendering controls.

Keyed by the canonical ``domain:resource.action`` id — unlike the rest of
this module, which keeps the axes structured. This payload is not a
description of authority to be reasoned about; it is a table a UI looks
entries up in, and it is looked up by the same id each route's permission
gate is named by. Structuring it would
force every lookup to re-assemble the string it is keyed on.

**Kind-level answers.** Each is the engine's decision with no target
instance. For an operation whose gate is instance-scoped, "not allowed" here
does not mean the caller is refused on every instance — consult that
resource's own capability flags instead.

NativeBotConfig.title: NativeBotConfig
NativeBotConfig.description:
Platform-level native bot config — input to broker prompt rendering.

Stored as JSONB in bots.desired_config when bot_type=native. The
``bot_type`` field is the discriminator for the BotConfig union.

``extra="ignore"`` mirrors OpenClawBotConfig: old data with removed

NativeConfigPatch.title: NativeConfigPatch
NativeConfigPatch.description:
Patchable fields for native bot configs.

Minimal by design: model ref + host policy + tool settings only.
Structure mirrors ``NativeBotConfig`` so ``patch_model()`` applies updates
recursively without manual field mapping.

The instructions are not here: a native bot's soul is a ``bot_files``
revision, edited through the file surfaces (PlatDev #3684). Unknown fields
are refused rather than ignored, so a client still sending the removed
instructions field gets a 422 instead of a silently dropped edit.

NativeLane.title: NativeLane
NativeLane.description: The six native lanes at cutover (#3734).

NativeLaneRefusal.title: NativeLaneRefusal
NativeLaneRefusal.description:
Why native owned mode refuses a credential, decided at config time (#3734 §5, #3809).

The one vocabulary for the config-time refusal: the API answers a native
bot's credential edit with it (``native_lane_refused``, 422) and L8c
exports it to the app. It is a fact about the credential's provider and
protocol only, never its model: every model of a served credential is
served, on the wire :func:`native_route_for` picks.

The runtime refusal stays the backstop, as the proto
``OWNED_REFUSAL_REASON_UNSUPPORTED_PROTOCOL``: a credential that changes
under a bot after the edit (an org-level credential edit) still cannot
reach the provider.

refused_links.description: Every usable LLM credential owned mode refuses, in chain order; the same shape the harness switch's lane_refused result carries

status.title: Status

detail.title: Detail

instance.description: Request path that produced the error

error_code.title: Error Code
