errors.title: Errors
errors.description: Field-level failures (present on 422 responses from validation)

trace_id.title: Trace Id
trace_id.description: OpenTelemetry trace ID (32 hex chars) when tracing is active. Lets support pivot from a failure the caller reports straight to the Tempo trace.

NativeLaneRefusedProblem.title: NativeLaneRefusedProblem
NativeLaneRefusedProblem.description:
422 ``native_lane_refused``: the body a native bot's refused credential edit gets.

Declared on every route that re-derives a native bot's chain
(:data:`NATIVE_LANE_REFUSED_RESPONSES`), so the generated client types
``refused_links`` and its :class:`~botyard_core.native.lanes.NativeLaneRefusal`
reasons instead of an untyped extension bag.

NativeToolCallPart.title: NativeToolCallPart
NativeToolCallPart.description:
A tool call to a native tool.

For native tools with a stable cross-provider shape (currently `tool_search`), this base
class can be promoted to a typed subclass with a narrowed `args` `TypedDict`. See
[`NativeToolSearchCallPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.NativeToolSearchCallPart] for the
canonical example.

Adding a typed subclass for a future native tool (see `pydantic_ai._tool_search` for
a worked example):

1. Add a sibling `pydantic_ai/_<name>.py` module that defines the cross-provider
   `TypedDict`s, the `NativeToolCallPart` / `NativeToolReturnPart` subclasses,
   and registers their narrowers into `_NATIVE_CALL_NARROWERS` /
   `_NATIVE_RETURN_NARROWERS` keyed by `tool_kind`. Subclass overrides
   `tool_kind: Literal['<emitter>']` to match the emitting
   [`AbstractNativeTool.kind`][pydantic_ai.native_tools.AbstractNativeTool.kind],
   and shadows `args` / `content` with a narrower type.
2. Late-import the new module from this file (alongside the existing tool-search
   import) so registration runs whenever `pydantic_ai.messages` is imported.
3. Add the subclass to `ModelResponsePart`'s discriminated union and to
   `_model_response_part_discriminator` so Pydantic deserialization auto-promotes
   on `model_validate` / `model_validate_json`.

Dispatch is by `tool_kind`, not `tool_name`. This protects users whose tools happen to
share a name with one of ours from accidentally getting their parts promoted (and
failing shape validation against the typed `args`/`content`).

The `provider_details` field carries genuinely non-portable provider extras
(e.g. Anthropic's `strategy: 'bm25' | 'regex'` for tool search). Promote a field
to a typed slot in `args` / `content` only when at least two of OpenAI, Anthropic,
and Google support it (cf. [issue #3885](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/issues/3885)).

MCP server tools land here with `tool_kind='mcp_server'` (label stays in
`tool_name='mcp_server:<label>'`); typed-subclass work for MCP is tracked by
[issue #3561](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/issues/3561).

NativeToolSearchCallPart-Input.title: NativeToolSearchCallPart
NativeToolSearchCallPart-Input.description:
Typed view of a [`NativeToolCallPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.NativeToolCallPart] for tool search.

Used on the native server-side tool-search path (Anthropic BM25/regex, OpenAI
Responses) where the provider executes the search and emits a native result.
The local-fallback path uses
[`ToolSearchCallPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.ToolSearchCallPart] instead.

To detect a tool-search part regardless of execution path (native server-side
vs. local fallback), check `part.tool_kind == 'tool-search'` — this works
across both call/return and both server/local variants.

Shadows `args` with a narrower type. The `str` variant covers the
streaming / partial-args case before parsing completes; once parsed,
`args` is a [`ToolSearchArgs`][pydantic_ai.messages.ToolSearchArgs]
`TypedDict`.

url.description: A path such as '/settings' or a full http(s) URL on the page's own origin. Any other origin is refused.

NavigateAction.title: NavigateAction
NavigateAction.description: Go to another URL on the same Bot Page. Must be the last action.

NoRecommendedModel.description: The pack recommends no model; the bot keeps the default.

user_id.title: User Id
user_id.description: Stable identifier of the authoring user.

avatar_url.title: Avatar Url
avatar_url.description: The author's current avatar URL, or null when they have none.

NotificationAuthor.title: NotificationAuthor
NotificationAuthor.description:
Org-safe display identity of the human who authored a notification.

Present only on human-authored kinds (``user_mention``) and only while the
author is still a member of the organization; bot-authored and platform
notifications carry ``author: null`` and are attributed to ``sender``.

dismissed_notification_ids.title: Dismissed Notification Ids
dismissed_notification_ids.description: Ids dismissed by this call; empty when there was nothing to dismiss.

NotificationDismissAllResponse.title: NotificationDismissAllResponse
NotificationDismissAllResponse.description: Result of dismissing every notification for the calling user.

sender.description: Authenticated sender identity, resolved within the notification organization.

author.description: Human who authored this notification (e.g. who @-mentioned you). Null for bot-authored and platform notifications, and once the author is no longer a member of the organization.

kind.description: Who authored this notification and therefore owns its lifecycle.

conversation_id.title: Conversation Id
conversation_id.description: Conversation whose human blockage this represents.

retry_request_id.title: Retry Request Id
retry_request_id.description: Request id of the failed turn, present only when re-sending it unchanged is a sensible recourse. Clients treat its presence as the gate for a retry affordance.

read_at.title: Read At
read_at.description: When the current user read it.

resolved_at.title: Resolved At
resolved_at.description: When it stopped requiring this user's attention.

NotificationItem.title: NotificationItem
NotificationItem.description: A notification projected with the current user's recipient state.

NotificationKind.title: NotificationKind
NotificationKind.description: Who authored a notification and therefore owns its lifecycle.

bot_id.title: Bot Id
bot_id.description: Stable identifier of the bot that sent the notification.

name.title: Name
name.description: Current bot display name, or null when the bot is unavailable.

slug.title: Slug
slug.description: Current bot slug, or null when the bot is unavailable.

avatar_url.title: Avatar Url
avatar_url.description: Current bot avatar URL, or null when the bot is unavailable.

is_available.title: Is Available
is_available.description: Whether the sender bot is currently available in this organization.

NotificationSender.title: NotificationSender
NotificationSender.description: Org-safe display identity for the authenticated bot that sent a notification.

recipients.title: Recipients
recipients.description: User ids to notify. Empty means the conversation's accountable human.

mode.description: on_change notifies only when the outcome class flips between ok and not_ok; every_run notifies on every matching outcome.

NotifyHumansAction.title: NotifyHumansAction
NotifyHumansAction.description: Notify humans in the schedule's conversation.

redirect_url.title: Redirect Url
redirect_url.description: Provider authorization URL to redirect the browser to

OAuthStartResponse.title: OAuthStartResponse
OAuthStartResponse.description: Response from OAuth start — contains redirect URL.

OAuthTokenSet.title: OAuthTokenSet
OAuthTokenSet.description:
An OAuth token pair, as pasted from a provider CLI's auth config.

Shared by the manual-token endpoint and by ``CredentialCreate.oauth_tokens``,
so both surfaces validate the same shape.

ObservedState.title: ObservedState
ObservedState.description:
Operator's view of where a bot is in the reconciler phase pipeline.

Phase sub-states (``provisioning:*`` / ``updating:*``) track progress
through the pipeline; see ``core.services.provisioner.reconciler`` for the
full state machine. Legacy bare ``provisioning`` / ``updating`` values are
retained for rollout safety and automatically route to ``*_INFRA`` when
encountered by the reconciler.

system_prompt_mode.title: System Prompt Mode
system_prompt_mode.description: System prompt source: botyard (lean, default) or openclaw

cli_watchdog.description: CLI backend reliability-watchdog overrides. Tunes when openclaw's claude-cli watchdog fires the no-output timeout that SIGKILLs the CLI session. Defaults are more generous than upstream so long silent bash tool calls (e.g. SQL queries) don't get killed.

tool_search.description: Tool Search. Defers tool schemas behind a search surface instead of inlining all of them in every prompt. Auto by default; owners can opt out per bot. Runtime-agnostic: config generation maps it to Claude Code's ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH on claude-cli bots and to OpenClaw's tools.toolSearch on embedded (pi) bots.

compaction.description: Context-compaction safeguards (serialized for v2026.6.1+). Defaults harden against overflow-induced stuck sessions.

context_limits.description: Context budget ceilings (serialized for v2026.6.1+). Caps a single live tool result so one large MCP response cannot dominate the window.

OpenClawBotConfig.title: OpenClawBotConfig
OpenClawBotConfig.description:
Platform-level bot config — the input to version-specific serialization.

Only includes fields that are platform-specific or that we explicitly
control. OpenClaw fills defaults for everything else at load time.

Stored as JSONB in bots.desired_config. The ``bot_type`` field acts as
the discriminator for a future union of bot-type configs.

``extra="ignore"`` ensures old data with removed fields doesn't break
on read (schema evolution safety).

tool_search.description: Tool Search — defers tool schemas behind a search surface instead of inlining every schema in the prompt. Runtime-agnostic: config generation maps it to Claude Code's ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH on claude-cli bots and to OpenClaw's tools.toolSearch on embedded (pi) bots.

thinking_default.title: Thinking Default
thinking_default.description: Default thinking budget level for conversations

reasoning_default.title: Reasoning Default
reasoning_default.description: Default reasoning mode (off, on, or stream)

system_prompt_mode.title: System Prompt Mode
system_prompt_mode.description: System prompt source: botyard (lean) or openclaw (default)

OpenClawConfigPatch.title: OpenClawConfigPatch
OpenClawConfigPatch.description:
Patchable fields for OpenClaw bot configs.

Structure mirrors ``OpenClawBotConfig`` so that ``patch_model()`` can
apply updates recursively. All fields are optional — only provided
fields are applied. Use ``model_fields_set`` to distinguish unset
from explicitly-set-to-None.

OperationResult.title: OperationResult
OperationResult.description: Result of a single migration operation.

OrgAppFilterField.title: OrgAppFilterField
OrgAppFilterField.description:
Filterable fields for the org-wide Bot Page list.

Deliberately small. ``kind`` is **not** filterable: the browser-session
exclusion is structural, and offering the column would invite a filter that
looks like it should be able to relax it. ``expires_at`` is not filterable
either — expiry is expressed by the ``include_expired`` scope flag, so there
is exactly one way to ask for expired rows.

``bot_id`` narrows the list to one bot's pages and accepts ``eq`` and
``in`` only. It can only narrow: filtering on a bot the caller cannot use,
or one outside this org, returns an empty list rather than an error, so the
response never reveals whether a bot exists.

slug.title: Slug
slug.description: Hostname label under the Bot Page base domain.

status.description: Exposure lifecycle status.

bot_id.title: Bot Id
bot_id.description: Identifier of the bot serving this exposure.

bot_slug.title: Bot Slug
bot_slug.description: Slug of the bot serving this exposure.

bot_name.title: Bot Name
bot_name.description: Display name of the bot serving this exposure.

bot_avatar_url.title: Bot Avatar Url
bot_avatar_url.description: Avatar of the bot serving this exposure, denormalised so the card renders identity from one response. Null when the bot has no avatar; the client falls back to the bot's initial. Required-but-nullable on purpose: with a default, a mapper that forgets to set it emits null silently, which is the exact regression this field was added to fix.

expires_at.title: Expires At
expires_at.description: Optional expiry timestamp; null means persistent until revoked.

last_seen_at.title: Last Seen At
last_seen_at.description: Last time the platform successfully routed a request to this exposure. Null for exposures not visited since request stamping began.

pinned.title: Pinned
pinned.description: Whether the calling user has pinned this Bot Page. Pins are per-user, so this is always false for API-key and bot principals.

OrgAppResponse.title: OrgAppResponse
OrgAppResponse.description:
One Bot Page tile on the org-wide Apps card.

Carries the owning bot inline so the card renders from a single response —
no follow-up request per row. There is deliberately **no** health field: the
bot-scoped surface probes health by exec'ing into the bot over the bridge
per exposure, which org-wide would be one round trip per tile on every page
load.

include_expired.title: Include Expired
include_expired.description: Include exposures whose expiry has passed. Revoked exposures and browser sessions are excluded regardless.

OrgAppSearchRequest.title: OrgAppSearchRequest
OrgAppSearchRequest.description:
Body for ``POST /orgs/{org_id}/apps/search``.

An empty body is the same request as ``GET /orgs/{org_id}/apps``.

unresolved.title: Unresolved
unresolved.description: Unresolved notifications for the user in this org.

OrgAttentionCount.description: How many notifications in one org still need the user.

not_found.description: Requested bot ids that are malformed, unknown, deleted, in another org, or not readable by the caller. The cases are not distinguished.

OrgBotPackInstalls.title: OrgBotPackInstalls
OrgBotPackInstalls.description: Installed packs and per-item provenance, per requested bot.

start_with_default_tools.title: Start With Default Tools
start_with_default_tools.description: Whether a bot created from this version also gets the platform's suggested default tools (true) or only the pack's own tools (false). No effect when installing onto an existing bot.

support.title: Support
support.description: What this version can run on each kind of bot, one entry per permitted hosting type and harness. Informational: an install skips unsupported items and never refuses.

OrgPackVersion.title: OrgPackVersion
OrgPackVersion.description: A published version with its soul and description: everything "view the pack" shows.

OrgPackVersions.title: OrgPackVersions

mfa_required.title: Mfa Required

OrgUpdate.title: OrgUpdate
OrgUpdate.description: Request to update an organization. Plan changes go through subscription endpoints.

series.title: Series

current.title: Current
current.description: Current count of resources counting toward this meter

included_units.title: Included Units
included_units.description: Units included per billing period at no extra charge (null = no gate on this plan)

hard_cap.title: Hard Cap
hard_cap.description: Absolute ceiling enforced at write time (null = no cap on this plan)

unit_price_cents.title: Unit Price Cents
unit_price_cents.description: Overage price per unit in cents (null = no overage billing)

OrgUsageMeter.title: OrgUsageMeter
OrgUsageMeter.description:
Live usage for one meter, joined with the active plan's gate (when any).

``current`` reflects the cap-enforcement count (active rows the user
can see in their lists), not the daily-snapshot value reported to the
billing provider — see
:mod:`~botyard_core.services.api.meter_counts` for why those differ.

``included_units`` is **null** when the active plan has no gate for
this meter (Enterprise / unlimited / internal plans). The FE reads
null as "no gate, free" and skips the overage/blocked banner. We
still emit ``current`` so plan-change projection can compare a
no-gate org's usage against a target plan that *does* have gates.

currency.title: Currency
currency.description: ISO 4217 currency code applied to every unit_price_cents in this snapshot

text_body.title: Text Body
text_body.description: Plain-text body hydrated from Resend, if available.

html_body.title: Html Body
html_body.description: HTML body hydrated from Resend, if available.

body_available.title: Body Available
body_available.description: True when the body was hydrated from Resend; False if it could not be fetched.

OutboundEmailRecord.title: OutboundEmailRecord
OutboundEmailRecord.description: Full sent email — metadata from our row + body hydrated from Resend.

OutboundEmailSearchRow.title: OutboundEmailSearchRow
OutboundEmailSearchRow.description: Token-lean projection of one sent email for the Sent list.

OutcomeActions.description: Terminal actions for an outcome. All omitted (``{}``) means do nothing.

OutcomeRouting.title: OutcomeRouting
OutcomeRouting.description:
What to do for one outcome: act now, or retry and act on ``then``.

With ``retry`` set, the terminal actions belong in ``then`` (applied once
retries run out), never beside ``retry``: actions next to a retry would be
ambiguous between "on every attempt" and "after the last one".

OwnedWire.title: OwnedWire
OwnedWire.description:
The upstream wire an owned step leaves on.

Preparation always runs in the Responses vocabulary the native lane
speaks; the wire is only how the finished request leaves and how its
answer is read back.

PackAvatarChoice.description: Whether an install onto an existing bot replaces its avatar (D16).

avatar_url.description: Avatar image URL — an image data URI (DiceBear SVG, or an uploaded WebP/PNG/JPEG) or an https:// URL. Max 16384 characters.

PackBotCustomAvatar.description: Start with this image instead of the pack's. It is the bot's own, not a pack item.

settings.description: Per pack setting: 'pack' (the default for a setting left out), 'keep' the bot's value, or a 'custom' value. Each path at most once, and only paths the pack sets.

connections.description: Per mcp_catalog_entry connection: 'use_server' binds the named org server; 'leave_pending' binds nothing, now or by later setup, until bound explicitly. A connection left out binds as before: the one visible server from its entry. Vault connections take no choice.

description.description: Short human-facing description / role for the bot (e.g. 'Platform developer'). Display metadata only — not injected into the bot's system prompt.

avatar.title: Avatar
avatar.description: 'pack' (the default) starts with the pack's avatar; 'custom' with your own.

PackBotRequest.description:
One bot to create from one pack version.

``settings`` and ``connections`` are the install choices of ``POST

value of its own to keep.

A Runtime Vault secret a pack needs the installing org to supply (D30).

A frozen subset of ``VaultInputSecretSpec``. **There is no value field, and
there never will be:** the value is entered into the buyer's own vault by
the install wizard (P4). ``extra="forbid"`` makes a value-shaped key a
validation error rather than something silently dropped or stored.

thinking_default.title: Thinking Default

reasoning_default.title: Reasoning Default

PackSettings.title: PackSettings
PackSettings.description:
The bot settings a pack may set: an explicit allow-list (J3).

Every field is a user-safe behaviour knob that an org member can already
change on their own bot, and each reuses the owner-facing patch type so the
accepted values cannot drift from what the config actually takes. ``None``
means "the pack does not set this".

**Never allowed, and absent on purpose:** ``host_policy``, credentials and
the LLM chain, provider keys, network or host access,
addons, anything owner-only, and **any heartbeat setting, cadence
included**. A heartbeat runs the bot autonomously on a timer; with a
publisher-written soul and the buyer's tools and credits, a publisher-set
cadence (as often as every 5 minutes) is recurring side effects and spend
the buyer never asked for. Periodic runs are schedules (D8, built in P7)
and must be an explicit owner choice at install, never applied from the
pack (review on PR #3973).

Adding a field here is a product decision (J3), not a convenience: it lets
content from a publisher change that setting on every bot that installs
the pack. Before adding one, ask whether it makes the bot *act* more often
or more widely; if so it is not a safe setting.

Permission.title: Permission
Permission.description:
A concrete capability: a fully-specified ``(domain, resource, action)``.

Frozen, so instances are hashable and compare by value — a stable identity
for matching, set membership, and audit. Construct one where it is needed
(``Permission(domain=Domain.PLATFORM, resource=Resource.FLEET, action=Action.READ)``);
there is no need to pre-declare it as a named enum member.

PermissionAction.title: PermissionAction
PermissionAction.description:
The permission ``action`` axis, as it appears on the wire.

A deliberate mirror of :class:`botyard_core.authz.permissions.Action`, and
the *only* axis that is mirrored — ``Domain`` and ``Resource`` are exposed
directly. The reason is a name collision, not a design preference:
``botyard_core.models.bridge.generated`` already contributes a class named
``Action`` to the OpenAPI components, and two schemas with one name make
Pydantic disambiguate **both** by fully-qualified module path. That would
rename the *bridge's* long-standing ``Action`` as collateral of an authz
change, and leave the generated TypeScript referring to
``botyard_core__authz__permissions__Action`` — a Python module path leaking
into the client API surface that every consumer of this endpoint would then
have to name.

Mirroring one enum is the smaller cost, and ``test_permission_action_matches_core``
makes the duplication safe: adding an action to the core vocabulary without
adding it here fails CI rather than silently producing an endpoint that
cannot express it.

PermissionCatalogueResponse.title: PermissionCatalogueResponse
PermissionCatalogueResponse.description:
Everything that can be granted — concrete permissions and wildcard scopes.

A **discriminated union on ``kind``**, and that is the load-bearing part.
Every wildcard shape has its own entry with its own ``id``, so a held grant
maps to exactly one entry whatever its shape: matching ``audit:*.*`` lands
on the domain-scope entry rather than fanning out across the six audit
leaves. Rendering a wildcard as a finite tick-list therefore stops being the
path of least resistance — which matters because such a render
**under-reports** reach, the dangerous direction on a security surface.

permissions.title: Permissions
permissions.description: Every requested permission, sorted and de-duplicated like the payload.

PermissionGrantApprovalDetails.title: PermissionGrantApprovalDetails
PermissionGrantApprovalDetails.description: ``permission.grant`` — every permission the ask names, in payload order.

PermissionGrantCreate.title: PermissionGrantCreate
PermissionGrantCreate.description:
Request to grant one permission pattern to one actor.

The grantee travels in the body rather than the path so the route stays a
flat collection (``POST /permission-grants``) instead of a four-segment
``/actors/{type}/{id}/permissions``.

PermissionHolderResponse.title: PermissionHolderResponse
PermissionHolderResponse.description:
One actor that holds a queried permission, and by what authority.

``scope`` is part of the answer, never a detail: the same permission triple
can be held over every instance of a type, over one named record, or over
everything belonging to one named record — and merging any of those reports a
narrow holder as holding broad authority.

Consumers must render **the three groups** distinguishably, grouping by
permission *and* shape and naming the members inside. ``scope_shape`` exists
so that does not require inspecting ``scope`` by hand, and so no consumer
invents a fourth answer.

**This is a list of holders, not a list of reachable objects.** A kind-level
holder here may still be refused an individual record by the ``INSTANCE_GATED``
gate — an ``org:viewer`` appears as a kind-level holder of ``bot:bot.read``
while a ``RESTRICTED`` bot stays invisible to it. Answering "who can reach
this bot?" from this payload alone overstates the set; the per-instance
question is ``PolicyEngine.check`` against that bot.

PermissionPatternPayload.title: PermissionPatternPayload
PermissionPatternPayload.description: A permission pattern on the wire. ``null`` on an axis means wildcard.

PermissionScopeShape.title: PermissionScopeShape
PermissionScopeShape.description:
*What* a held permission applies to — the shape of the authority.

Three answers, because there are three genuinely different things an actor can
hold and a boolean can express two. Reporting one as another is the failure
this vocabulary exists to prevent: the question is asked during an incident,
to decide whose access to cut off.

``KIND_LEVEL``
    Every instance of the resource type. ``org:viewer`` reading any bot.
``INSTANCE``
    **One record that already exists.** A bot's self grant over its own row.
``ANCHORED``
    **Everything belonging to one named record** — an open-ended set that
    grows on its own. "May post in the conversations of bot X" also covers a
    conversation created tomorrow.

``INSTANCE`` and ``ANCHORED`` both name exactly one bot, so they read
identically on screen while meaning different things. Rendering ``ANCHORED``
as ``INSTANCE`` understates it — the dangerous direction, and the same
understatement that made merging scoped holders with kind-level ones a
wrong-but-authoritative answer to "who can reach admin?".

**``ANCHORED`` is declared before anything emits it, deliberately.** Anchored
scope arrives with Phase 2 (platform-development task 1607); declaring the
value now means every consumer handles it from the day it first appears, and
Phase 2 is then purely additive. Adding a third value to a two-valued field
*after* a UI is built on it is a breaking change on a security surface.

PermissionSource.title: PermissionSource
PermissionSource.description:
Which authority put a permission on an actor.

Five authorities, distinguished by **who can change them** — which is the
only distinction a permissions view exists to make:

``ROLE_BUNDLE``
    The code-defined floor in :data:`~botyard_core.authz.roles.ROLE_PERMISSIONS`.
    Changed by shipping code, never by a grant. Not revocable through this
    surface; the way to remove it is to change the actor's *role*.
``ROLE_DELTA``
    A ``role_permissions`` row — an org's addition on top of the floor.
    Revocable, but it affects **everyone holding the role**, not this actor.
``ACTOR_GRANT``
    An ``actor_grants`` row for this actor specifically. The only source a
    per-actor revoke acts on.
``SELF_GRANT``
    The permanent, instance-scoped grant a bot holds over its own record.
    Code-defined and never persisted, so there is no row to delete.
``RESOURCE_MEMBER``
    Instance-scoped authority synthesised from a ``resource_members`` row by
    ``RESOURCE_ROLE_BUNDLES`` (#2940). Also never persisted as a grant, so
    there is no grant row to delete — the way to remove it is to change or
    remove the *membership*, which is why it must not render as revocable
    here: the delete button would point at the wrong table.

``ROLE_BUNDLE``, ``SELF_GRANT`` and ``RESOURCE_MEMBER`` are therefore **not
revocable**, and a UI must render them as such rather than as a grant with a
missing delete button — an action that reports success and changes nothing is
worse than no action.

The MCP audit path's flat ``grant_source`` label (``org_viewer``,
``org_bot_default``, ...) is derivable from ``(source, role_key)``, so the
two surfaces stay reconcilable instead of forking into a third vocabulary.

PlanFeature.title: PlanFeature
PlanFeature.description: Feature gates enabled by a subscription plan.

included_units.title: Included Units
included_units.description: Units granted per billing period at no extra charge (0 = none)

hard_cap.title: Hard Cap
hard_cap.description: Absolute ceiling enforced at write time (null = no cap)

unit_price_cents.title: Unit Price Cents
unit_price_cents.description: Overage price per metered unit, in cents (null = no overage billing)

PlanMeterGateItem.title: PlanMeterGateItem
PlanMeterGateItem.description:
One gate on a plan: included units, optional hard cap, optional overage price.

Carries every gate on the plan — both count meters (bots/seats/MCP) and
resource-overage meters (cpu/memory/storage). Both bill the same way: the
average unit held over the billing period x ``unit_price_cents`` (whole-cent
€/unit-month). Consumers distinguish the two by ``meter_key`` (overage keys
are :data:`~botyard_core.models.enums.RESOURCE_OVERAGE_METER_KEYS`); overage
gates carry no ``hard_cap`` so the count-only consumers already skip them.

PlanResponse.title: PlanResponse
PlanResponse.description:
Plan response.

``meter_gates`` carries every gate on the plan — both count meters
(bots/seats/MCP) and resource-overage meters (cpu/memory/storage), priced
uniformly in integer cents per unit per month. Consumers distinguish the two
by ``meter_key`` (overage keys are ``RESOURCE_OVERAGE_METER_KEYS``); overage
gates carry no ``hard_cap``, so cap/count-only consumers already skip them.

``resource_defaults`` is the plan's per-consumer *included* resource
baseline, bucketed by consumer type (e.g. ``{"bot": {...}}``). It is the
floor billed at no charge: a consumer's metered resource overage is
``max(0, reserved - included)`` per line-item, so the UI needs this baseline
to project the overage cost of a resource change before applying it.

``resource_maximums`` is the plan's per-consumer *hard ceiling*, bucketed the
same way. It is SPARSE: each set line-item caps that dimension (the API
rejects a bot whose resolved resources exceed it with a 422); an absent
line-item — or an absent consumer, or an empty map — is uncapped. Distinct
from the overage gates (which *price* allocation above the included baseline)
— this is the absolute limit that can't be exceeded at any price, so the UI
needs it to warn (and block) before a user tries to save an over-limit value.

``billing_provider_free_product_id`` is the plan's *card-free* product
variant when it has one (a fixed-price €0 product carrying no metered
prices — the only shape the provider will check out without collecting a
payment method). It is exposed alongside the other provider product IDs so a
client can tell which variant a subscription sits on; see
``SubscriptionResponse.is_card_free``, which is the derived answer clients
should actually branch on.

PlatformRole.title: PlatformRole
PlatformRole.description:
Role an actor holds on the platform team.

Starts with a single ``ADMIN`` tier (full platform-admin access). Modelled
as a first-class enum rather than a bare boolean so the platform team can
grow non-admin tiers (e.g. read-only support) without a schema change.

Platform-team members are identified by the shared :class:`ActorType` /
actor-id vocabulary, constrained to ``USER`` and ``BOT`` (an API key is a
credential, not a grantable team member — enforced by a DB CHECK).

actor_type.description: Kind of actor being granted (user or bot)

actor_id.title: Actor Id
actor_id.description: ID of the actor (users.user_id or bots.id)

role.description: Platform role to grant (currently only admin)

PlatformTeamGrantRequest.title: PlatformTeamGrantRequest
PlatformTeamGrantRequest.description: Request to grant (or update the role of) a platform-team member.

PlatformTeamGrantedContent.title: PlatformTeamGrantedContent
PlatformTeamGrantedContent.description:
Typed content for granting an actor platform-team access.

Emitted when a human platform admin adds a user or bot to the platform team
(or changes an existing member's role). Bots can never manage the team, so
the initiating actor is always a human, attributed via the event ``user_id``.
``actor_type`` / ``actor_id`` identify the grantee; ``role`` is the granted
platform role; ``previous_role`` is set when this grant updated an existing
membership's role rather than creating a new one.

granted_by_user_id.title: Granted By User Id
granted_by_user_id.description: Human admin who created the grant; null for bootstrap rows

PlatformTeamRevokedContent.title: PlatformTeamRevokedContent
PlatformTeamRevokedContent.description:
Typed content for revoking an actor's platform-team access.

Emitted when a human platform admin removes a user or bot from the platform
team. ``actor_type`` / ``actor_id`` identify the removed actor;
``previous_role`` is the role they held before revocation.

Deliberately **identity-only**: unlike :class:`MyOrgResponse` it carries no
billing/plan/subscription fields (``plan_name`` / ``subscription_status`` /
``is_active``). ``/v1/me/orgs`` serves any principal — including bot and
API-key service actors — so it must not disclose the org's billing or
plan-active state to a non-user session. It exposes only what a caller needs
to resolve its own org context (id, slug, name, status, MFA requirement, and
the caller's role). The human billing view stays on the user-only
``/v1/users/me/orgs`` (``MyOrgResponse``).

type.title: Type
type.description: URI identifier for the problem type; primary machine identifier. Clients should switch on this (or ``error_code``), not on ``title`` or ``detail``.

ProblemDetails.title: ProblemDetails
ProblemDetails.description:
RFC 9457 Problem Details response body.

Every Botyard error response is a ``ProblemDetails`` serialized as
``application/problem+json``. The five RFC core fields are always
populated; the three Botyard extensions (``error_code``, ``errors``,
``trace_id``) appear as described below.

pointer.title: Pointer
pointer.description: RFC 6901 JSON Pointer into the request body (e.g. '/config/model/primary'). Empty string '' points at the root document.

ProblemErrorItem.title: ProblemErrorItem
ProblemErrorItem.description:
Field-level problem, carried inside :attr:`ProblemDetails.errors`.

Conforms to the conventions described in RFC 9457 §3.1 for extension
members that describe individual request-field failures. The
``pointer`` is an RFC 6901 JSON Pointer into the request body so the
client can navigate exactly which field failed.

ProcessWatchOutcome.title: ProcessWatchOutcome
ProcessWatchOutcome.description:
Why a process watch resolved — and the outcome the wake announces.

``wake_on`` selects which of these the bot wants to be woken for; the
outcome is always recorded even when no wake was requested for it, so the
watch history explains itself.

- ``EXIT_SUCCESS`` — the process exited 0.
- ``EXIT_FAILURE`` — the process exited non-zero, or was killed by a signal.
- ``EXIT_UNOBSERVED`` — the process is gone, but its exit status could not be
  read. Only reachable for a ``PID`` attach: the watcher was never that
  process's parent, so there is no status left for it to collect. This is a
  distinct outcome rather than a guess at one of the two above, because the
  alternative is for the bridge to *invent* a status — and inventing
  ``EXIT_SUCCESS`` in particular yields a confident "your job finished" for
  a job that may have crashed. A bot that needs the real status should have
  the bridge spawn the work (``COMMAND``) rather than attach to it.
- ``TIMEOUT`` — ``deadline_at`` passed with the process still running.
- ``RUNTIME_RESTART`` — the bot runtime restarted, so both the watched
  process and the in-pod waiter are gone. Detected platform-side by lease
  expiry, because by construction nothing in the pod survives to report it.
  A bot receiving this should treat the work as lost and re-arm.

ProcessWatchState.title: ProcessWatchState
ProcessWatchState.description:
Lifecycle state of a process watch.

The state column is the concurrency primitive: exactly-once wake delivery
is a conditional ``ARMED -> FIRING`` transition, so a bridge-reported exit
and the worker's deadline sweep can race freely and only one of them wins
the claim.

- ``ARMED`` — live; the bridge is expected to be holding a lease.
- ``FIRING`` — claimed by exactly one deliverer; the wake is in flight.
- ``FIRED`` — terminal; the wake was delivered (see ``outcome``).
- ``CANCELLED`` — terminal; the bot withdrew the watch before it resolved.
- ``UNDELIVERABLE`` — terminal; the watch resolved but the wake could not
  be delivered even after retries. Distinct from ``FIRED`` so a silent
  non-wake is visible rather than indistinguishable from success.

ProcessWatchStopMode.title: ProcessWatchStopMode
ProcessWatchStopMode.description:
Whether cancelling a watch also signals the process, and with which signal.

``none`` leaves it running; ``sigterm`` asks it to stop and lets it clean
up; ``sigkill`` asks the kernel to end it outright. Signals are delivered,
not awaited: read ``stop_result`` before reporting that anything stopped.

ProcessWatchStopResult.title: ProcessWatchStopResult
ProcessWatchStopResult.description:
What a requested stop actually achieved.

- ``not_requested`` — no stop was asked for, so none was attempted.
- ``signalled`` — the signal was delivered. Delivery only: nothing waited
  for the process to exit, so do not report it as stopped on this alone.
- ``not_running`` — already finished, or gone before the signal landed.
  The only value that means the process is certainly not running.
- ``not_held`` — the runtime was not holding the watch and had nothing to
  signal; the process may still be running out of its reach.
- ``identity_lost`` — the pid no longer identifies the watched process, so
  signalling was refused; it may still be running.
- ``failed`` — signalling errored; assume it is still running.

The card's read model. Served by ``GET …/questions/{id}`` to every viewer with

QuestionRequestStatus.description:
Lifecycle status of a bot-initiated question asked in a conversation.

Deliberately **not** ``pending``/``submitted``. A question may be answered by
more than one respondent, so "has it been answered" is not a property of the
request — it is derived per respondent from that person's answer rows. What
the request itself tracks is only whether it still accepts answers:

``OPEN``
  Accepting answers. The default and, absent an explicit close, the state a
  question stays in forever — a question does **not** expire on a timer,
  because answering one after a long absence is a feature of an asynchronous
  ask, not a failure mode. A bot may set an explicit ``expires_at`` when an
  ask is genuinely time-boxed.
``CLOSED``
  The bot got what it needed and stopped accepting answers. Terminal.
``CANCELLED``
  The bot withdrew the question (it moved on, the work changed). Terminal,
  and distinct from ``CLOSED`` because the card renders it differently: a
  closed question was answered enough, a cancelled one never will be.

RequirementStatus.title: RequirementStatus
RequirementStatus.description:
How one tool requirement stands against what an actor holds.

Five values rather than the obvious three, because two of the cases that
*look* like "this tool needs nothing" are not that at all, and collapsing
either into :attr:`NOT_REQUIRED` produces a surface that is confidently wrong.

``SELF_SCOPED``
    The requirement targets the bot's own record and is satisfied by the
    permanent, code-defined self grant. It is **not promptable and not
    revocable** — there is no row behind it — so it must never reach a
    permission prompt or a revoke cascade. It is reported rather than
    silently dropped: a requirement that vanishes from the response is
    indistinguishable from one nobody declared, and this surface exists to
    make declarations legible.
``CATALOG_UNMAPPED``
    The tool declares nothing, but it is a platform botyard-MCP tool and all
    of those *are* annotated — so the catalog has not been seeded since the
    annotations landed. Platform tool seeding is manual, which makes this a
    real operational window rather than a theoretical one. Reported as a
    degraded state so the assign flow can refuse to reassure; if it were
    folded into ``NOT_REQUIRED`` an unseeded catalog would report the entire
    tool surface as unconstrained and the prompt would ask for nothing while
    looking perfectly healthy.

coincide for most resources (``task``, ``bot``) and differ only for

The allocation ledger is polymorphic over consumers: a bot today, an

consumer kind is a one-line ``ALTER TYPE ... ADD VALUE`` migration.

ResourceQuantities.title: ResourceQuantities
ResourceQuantities.description:
A set of resource line-items as K8s quantities, keyed by metered resource.

Used in two roles, distinguished only by completeness:

* **Plan defaults** (``Plan.resource_defaults[consumer]``) — a complete base
  bundle: every billable ceiling (``cpu_limit`` / ``memory_limit`` /
  ``storage``) set; requests optional (burstable-derived when omitted). There
  is no global fallback — a consumer that can't resolve a complete bundle is
  an invariant break (see ``ResourceDefaultsUnavailableError``).

mode.title: Mode
mode.description: Per-org scanner mode override.  None → fall back to the service's global SCANNER_MODE env var (default: redact).  redact splices matched secrets out of the outbound body in flight and forwards the request; strict does the same but fails-closed (503) on scanner infrastructure errors; log_only audits matches without mutating or blocking the request (opt-in — the secret reaches upstream).

ScannerSettings.title: ScannerSettings
ScannerSettings.description:
Typed exfiltration-scanner settings for an org.

Write access is restricted to org owners.  Enterprise tenants need
to control scanner enforcement themselves.  The corresponding attack
vector — a compromised owner credential weakening enforcement — is
mitigated at the access layer (MFA, audit logs on the org_settings
table) rather than by hiding the control entirely.

Three modes (``log_only`` retained as an opt-in safety valve
alongside the redaction modes — see migration ``scanredact01`` and #256):

- ``redact`` (default) — on a match, the matched secret occurrences
  are spliced out of the **outbound request body in flight** and
  replaced with a ``[redacted:<key_path>]`` placeholder, then the
  request is forwarded.  The secret never reaches the upstream
  provider, and the conversation keeps working (no "poison-pill"
  where a leaked value re-trips a hard block on every subsequent
  turn).  A secret detected in an anomalous vector (custom header,
  URL path/query) is still **blocked** — there is no benign
  redact-and-continue story for that.  Scanner infrastructure errors
  fail **open** (request allowed) so a scanner outage can't take down
  legitimate traffic.
- ``strict`` — identical match handling (redact body, block anomalous
  vectors), but scanner infrastructure errors fail **closed** (503).
  For high-assurance workloads that prefer to fail a request rather
  than forward it unscanned.
- ``log_only`` — a match is **audited but not acted on**: the body is
  not mutated and the request is forwarded unchanged.  This is the
  safety valve for false positives (redaction mutates the payload, so
  a benign string colliding with a secret value would otherwise garble
  a legitimate request) and for rollout / investigation.  It is the
  one mode that lets the secret reach upstream, so it is strictly
  opt-in; the service default stays ``redact``.

ScheduleCatchupPolicy.title: ScheduleCatchupPolicy
ScheduleCatchupPolicy.description:
What to do with fires missed while the bot/engine was unavailable.

``SKIP`` drops missed occurrences entirely. ``RUN_ONCE_ON_RECOVERY`` fires
a single catch-up run when the target becomes reachable again, regardless
of how many occurrences were missed (no thundering backlog).

ScheduleCommandOutcome.title: ScheduleCommandOutcome
ScheduleCommandOutcome.description:
How one attempt of a scheduled command resolved (PlatDev #3357).

- ``SUCCESS`` / ``FAILURE`` — the process exited and ``exit_codes``
  classified its code (a signal kill counts as ``FAILURE``).
- ``TIMEOUT`` — the per-attempt ``timeout_seconds`` deadline passed.
- ``LOST`` — the runtime restarted underneath the run; nothing observed the
  exit.
- ``MISSED`` — the runtime could not be reached to start the run.
- ``SECRET_UNAVAILABLE`` — a ``secret_env`` key path could not be resolved
  at spawn, so the command never ran.
- ``SKIPPED_OVERLAP`` — another run held the ``concurrency_group`` lock and
  the overlap policy is ``skip``.
- ``DEFERRED`` — the command exited with a code ``exit_codes`` maps to
  ``deferred`` ("not ready yet") and the schedule's ``window`` still had
  room, so a recheck of the same occurrence was queued (PlatDev #4119).
  Health-neutral and never routed.
- ``LATE`` — the command was still deferring when the occurrence's window
  closed (or the next period fired first), so the period ended without a
  success. Terminal; routed via ``on_outcome.late``.

ScheduleFireStatus.title: ScheduleFireStatus
ScheduleFireStatus.description:
Terminal (or in-flight) status of a single schedule fire attempt.

Recorded in ``schedule_fires`` (the scheduler-postgres history table) for
external run tracking.

- ``PENDING`` — durable occurrence intent exists, but no delivery process
  owns it yet.
- ``FIRING`` — a delivery process owns the occurrence. If that process dies,
  the recovery sweep terminalizes the ambiguous attempt instead of blindly
  replaying a prompt that may already have caused external side effects.
- ``DELIVERED`` — the wake reached chat-proxy (and, for await-reply, a
  reply was collected).
- ``SKIPPED_BUSY`` — ``skip_if_busy`` rejected the fire because the
  conversation already had an active/queued turn. Deliberate, not a misfire.
- ``MISSED`` — the bot's WS never (re)connected within ``bot_wait_s``, so
  chat-proxy could not deliver the wake. This is a true misfire.
- ``FAILED`` — delivery was attempted but errored (e.g. await-reply timed
  out waiting on the bot, or an unexpected proxy error).
- ``SKIPPED_STALE`` — the occurrence was dropped by the SKIP-catchup
  staleness gate: Prefect executed it Late (its ``scheduled_for`` is older
  than the configured staleness horizon), so the worker deliberately did
  not deliver it. Like ``SKIPPED_BUSY`` this is a purposeful skip, not a
  misfire — recording it lets the catch-up reconciler tell "intentionally
  dropped" apart from "never attempted".

ScheduleRunStatus.title: ScheduleRunStatus
ScheduleRunStatus.description:
Normalised status of one schedule *run* (PlatDev #4203).

A run is one occurrence or manual trigger, whatever its kind. This folds the
prompt fire's ``ScheduleFireStatus`` and the command attempts' final
``ScheduleCommandOutcome`` into one vocabulary for the schedules UI:

- ``SUCCEEDED`` — did its job (command exited OK / bot woken).
- ``FAILED`` — errored, timed out, lost, missed, window closed, secret
  unavailable, or never started.
- ``SKIPPED`` — deliberately not run: bot busy, previous run still going,
  stale catch-up, or a window recheck closed without running.
- ``RUNNING`` — in flight.
- ``WAITING`` — a command between attempts: a "not ready" recheck or a
  failure retry is queued for ``next_check_at``.

strip.description: How to draw the schedule's history strip. A schedule firing every 6 h or slower (or with no estimable cadence) gets kind `runs`: draw `recent_runs`, one block per run. A faster one gets kind `buckets`: 30 buckets, each the smallest of 1/2/3/6 h that is at least the cadence, aligned to the schedule's timezone and coloured by the worst status inside. The cadence is the mean gap between the schedule's upcoming fires over the next 7 days.

ScheduleSpecKind.title: ScheduleSpecKind
ScheduleSpecKind.description:
How a schedule's firing times are specified (EPIC #493).

The full domain is modeled from day one even though only ``CRON`` is wired
into the engine first — so no schema migration is needed when the other
kinds come online.

- ``CRON`` — a cron expression (``spec.cron``).
- ``INTERVAL`` — a fixed period in seconds plus an anchor
  (``spec.interval_seconds`` + ``spec.anchor``).
- ``RRULE`` — an iCalendar RFC 5545 recurrence rule (``spec.rrule``),
  the native bi-weekly/complex-recurrence path Prefect gives us.
- ``EVENT`` — fired by an external event/webhook selector rather than a
  wall-clock time (``spec.event``).

ScheduleTriggerSource.title: ScheduleTriggerSource
ScheduleTriggerSource.description:
What caused a ``schedule_fires`` row to exist.

- ``SCHEDULED`` — the scheduler engine (Prefect) handed the worker an
  occurrence on the schedule's own cadence.
- ``MANUAL`` — a human (or agent) pressed "run now"; an out-of-band fire
  that does not belong to the schedule's cadence.

This is *load-bearing*, not merely descriptive. The ``(schedule_id,
scheduled_for)`` uniqueness that makes scheduled delivery idempotent under
the engine's at-least-once semantics is a **partial** unique index scoped to
``SCHEDULED`` rows. Scheduled claims therefore still contend on exactly the
same key — the dedupe guarantee is unchanged — while manual fires, which
have no idempotency requirement and may legitimately repeat, sit outside the
index entirely and can never squat an occurrence's claim slot.

raw payload, no secret value, no key path in content (the envelope
``resource_id`` carries the key path).  ``occurrences`` records how
many spans were redacted so ops can see the magnitude of a leak
without storing the leaked bytes.

This part is a member of both [`ModelRequestPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.ModelRequestPart] and
[`ModelResponsePart`][pydantic_ai.messages.ModelResponsePart], distinguished by `speaker`:
in `ModelRequest.parts` the speaker is always `'user'`; in `ModelResponse.parts` it is always

Standard (non-realtime) models can't consume this part directly; when history containing it is
used in an agent run, [`Model.prepare_messages`][pydantic_ai.models.Model.prepare_messages]
converts user-speaker parts to [`UserPromptPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.UserPromptPart]s and
assistant-speaker parts to [`TextPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.TextPart]s.

SubscriptionResponse.title: SubscriptionResponse
SubscriptionResponse.description:
Current billing subscription for an organization.

``billing_provider_product_id`` records *which* product variant of the plan
the subscription actually sits on. A plan may materialise as two products —
the ordinary metered one and a card-free €0 variant — so the plan alone does
not tell you whether a payment method was ever collected.

``is_card_free`` is the derived answer, and the one clients should branch
on. It mirrors the ``subscription_is_free`` predicate that
``SubscriptionService.select_plan`` uses server-side to decide whether a
move off this subscription must go through a card-collecting checkout
instead of an in-place product change. Deriving it here keeps that rule in
one place: a client that re-implemented the comparison and got it wrong
would let an org add billable resources with no card on file, which ends in
``past_due`` and dunning.

TaskBlockState.title: TaskBlockState
TaskBlockState.description:
The **current** renderable state of a task, resolved by the serving endpoint.

This is the rich card content a :class:`TaskContentBlock` refers to. It is
returned *only* by the member-gated content-block ``task`` endpoint (never
embedded in the conversation payload), so a viewer sees these fields only
after workforce ``VIEW`` membership is established. Server-resolved from the
real task, so the values are trustworthy rather than bot-supplied.

Carries the reference fields too (``org_slug`` / ``workforce_slug`` /
``workforce_name`` / ``task_number``) so the rendered card has everything it
needs — crumb, deeplink, and content — from a single fetch.

Records that the set of tools available to the model changed at this point.

Additions only. Withdrawing a tool is not supported yet, because no provider can be told about one

reference to a tool the request doesn't declare, so a withdrawn tool has to leave the `tools`

removals can join once they can be done cache-safely — see

ToolOutputChunkEvent.title: ToolOutputChunkEvent

Live chunk of tool output emitted while a tool is still running.

Carries the originating ``tool_call_id`` so renderers can attach the
progress text to the corresponding ``builtin-tool-call`` / eventual
``builtin-tool-return`` part. Wire-only — never persisted. The
canonical record is the ``builtin-tool-return`` ``part_end`` emitted
when the tool finishes; chunks fill the gap that pydantic-ai's part
schema leaves open (no streaming-delta primitive exists for tool
return content — see https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai/issues/1560
and pydantic-ai 2.x's removal of ``BuiltinToolResultEvent``).

ToolResourceKind.title: ToolResourceKind
ToolResourceKind.description:
Which resource a tool's permission check targets.

``SELF_BOT`` is the shape roughly half the tool surface needs: the tool acts
on the calling bot's own record (its config, files, memory, services,
schedules...). Resolving it to a concrete resource reference is what makes
the self grant instance-scoped, so a tool that resolves the *wrong* bot id is
denied.

Part of the shared vocabulary rather than the MCP service because the
distinction is load-bearing on the *product* side too: the self grant is
permanent and not user-managed, so a ``SELF_BOT`` tool can never be the
subject of a permission prompt or a revoke cascade. A surface that cannot see
this axis cannot implement that exemption.

ToolRuntime.title: ToolRuntime
ToolRuntime.description:
Where a tool executes — determines enforcement mechanism.

Each member names a *different* enforcement point, which is the bar a new
member has to clear. The value appears in every
:meth:`ToolCatalog.build_slug` result, so it is a durable public contract:
``mcp:botyard:send_email``, ``openclaw::exec``, ``native::file_read``.

* ``mcp`` — the platform serves the tool over MCP. Enforcement is in the
  gateway, which is also why these rows are reachable from every harness.
* ``openclaw`` — the identifier of a builtin compiled into the OpenClaw
  agent. The platform serves nothing; enforcement is writing the agent's
  own config (``tools.allow``).
* ``native`` — the identifier of a builtin compiled into ``botyardd``, the
  native runtime daemon. The platform serves nothing here either, and the
  gateway never sees the call: the daemon intercepts every ``host_*`` name
  before it reaches upstream. Enforcement is the daemon's own
  ``HostPolicy`` (``runtime/botyard-runtime/src/host_tools/policy.rs``),
  which fails closed by default.

``native`` is deliberately *not* folded into ``openclaw``. The two are the
same **shape** — a builtin, enforced by configuring the agent that owns it —
but they are different agents, and :data:`~botyard_core.hosting.
_HARNESS_TOOL_RUNTIMES` is keyed on this value. Reusing ``openclaw`` would
advertise ``file_read`` to OpenClaw bots, where the name means nothing.

ToolSearchCallPart-Input.title: ToolSearchCallPart
ToolSearchCallPart-Input.description:
Typed view of a [`ToolCallPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.ToolCallPart] for the local `search_tools` function call.

Used on the local-fallback path (and as the synthetic-injection target on
non-native providers receiving cross-provider history). The native server-side
path uses
[`NativeToolSearchCallPart`][pydantic_ai.messages.NativeToolSearchCallPart]

streaming / partial-args case before parsing completes; once parsed,
`args` is a [`ToolSearchArgs`][pydantic_ai.messages.ToolSearchArgs]
`TypedDict`.

mode.title: Mode
mode.description: ``always`` defers tool schemas on every turn; ``auto`` defers only above ``auto_threshold_percent``; ``off`` never defers. On the claude-cli runtime these are Claude Code's ``tst`` / ``tst-auto`` / ``standard``, emitted explicitly in all three cases because leaving the env var unset lets the CLI's non-first-party base-URL gate decide for us. OpenClaw's embedded Tool Search has no threshold mechanism, so ``auto`` behaves like ``always`` there.

auto_threshold_percent.title: Auto Threshold Percent
auto_threshold_percent.description: Percentage of the context window the deferrable tool schemas must exceed before ``auto`` mode defers them. Matches Claude Code's own default. Read only when ``mode`` is ``auto`` on the claude-cli runtime — OpenClaw's embedded Tool Search exposes no equivalent knob. Kept non-nullable so switching modes back and forth through a config patch never leaves an unrepresentable state.

ToolSearchConfig.title: ToolSearchConfig
ToolSearchConfig.description:
Tool Search: defer tool schemas out of the prompt behind a search surface.

One runtime-agnostic setting for one user-facing concept. The *mechanism*
differs per agent runtime, and the runtime is derived from the primary
model ref's provider rather than chosen by the owner — so asking the owner
to pick the right per-runtime switch would be asking about an
implementation detail they cannot see. Config generation does the mapping:

==================  ===================================================
runtime             mechanism
==================  ===================================================
``claude-cli``      ``cliBackends.claude-cli.env.ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH`` =
                    ``"true"`` / ``"auto:N"`` / ``"false"``
``pi`` (embedded)   ``tools.toolSearch`` =
                    ``{"enabled": true, "mode": "tools"}``, or absent
==================  ===================================================

With it on, the runtime withholds tool *schemas* from the prompt and
exposes a search surface instead; the model searches (or selects by exact
name) and then calls the real tool. Measured against the real Botyard
catalogue: 117,933 -> 43,863 input tokens (-62.8%) on ``claude-cli``, and
85,317 -> 15,719 (-82%) on the embedded loop.

Runtime-specific caveats worth knowing before turning this on:

* **claude-cli.** We set ``ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH`` explicitly rather than
  relying on Claude Code's default. The CLI's default mode is on, but it
  *self-disables* whenever ``ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`` is not a first-party
  Anthropic host, logging "...is not a first-party Anthropic host. Set
  ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true (or auto / auto:N) if your proxy forwards
  tool_reference blocks." Every Botyard bot points at the bridge's
  loopback stream-proxy, so the feature is off fleet-wide unless we opt
  in. Our proxy chain does forward the ``anthropic-beta`` header and
  ``tool_reference`` blocks — verified end-to-end with a full
  search-then-call round trip. Requires a model supporting
  ``tool_reference`` (Sonnet 4+ / Opus 4+); haiku is on Claude Code's
  unsupported list and silently keeps the full catalog, which is safe —
  just not cheaper.
* **pi (embedded).** OpenClaw's ``tools.toolSearch`` applies to embedded
  runs only; a CLI backend never reaches that code path, since it hands
  our ``mcp.servers`` verbatim to the CLI, which then talks to the Botyard
  MCP server directly. We select ``mode: "tools"`` — the structured
  search/describe/call surface — which is the mode that was measured.

**Defaults to auto.** Claude Code defers only when the deferrable schemas
exceed 10% of the context window. OpenClaw's embedded runtime has no
threshold mechanism, so the runtime mapping treats ``auto`` as enabled.
Owners can still select ``off`` explicitly from the bot detail page.

mode.title: Mode
mode.description: always (defer every turn) | auto (defer above the threshold) | off (never defer). Applies whatever mechanism the bot's runtime uses — Claude Code's ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH on claude-cli bots, OpenClaw's tools.toolSearch on embedded (pi) bots.

auto_threshold_percent.title: Auto Threshold Percent
auto_threshold_percent.description: Percentage of the context window the tool schemas must exceed before ``auto`` mode defers them. Ignored unless mode is auto, and read only on the claude-cli runtime — OpenClaw's embedded Tool Search has no threshold knob, so auto behaves like always there.

ToolSearchConfigPatch.title: ToolSearchConfigPatch
ToolSearchConfigPatch.description:
Patchable Tool Search fields.

Both fields are non-nullable on the target config, so ``None`` here means
"no change" with no ambiguity — and because ``mode`` alone decides the
behaviour, every state is reachable from every other state with a single
patch. Setting ``mode`` back to ``always`` or ``off`` does not require
clearing the threshold first.

TurnStatus.title: TurnStatus
TurnStatus.description:
Lifecycle state of a user message's turn within the steer/queue engine.

Persisted on the user ``conversation_messages`` row so the queue/steer
lifecycle survives a reload (it is otherwise derived live from Centrifugo
events on the client). ``None`` (the column default) means an ordinary turn
that was sent and answered without ever queueing or steering — the common
case — so the column stays sparse.

``QUEUED`` is strictly transient: every queued turn has its own request and
publish loop, which always reaches a terminal frame, so the row is never
left ``QUEUED`` once that loop ends. The stored DB value is the member name
(e.g. ``QUEUED``); the lowercase value is what serializes to clients.

``DEQUEUED`` is named for the ``chat.dequeued`` frame that triggers it — a
turn that *was* queued and has since been released to run. It is distinct
from the frontend's transient ``userTurnStatus="picked_up"`` (the universal
"bot is actively processing this turn" state, re-derived live from the
active-turn lease) — that state is never persisted here.

``CANCELLED`` is terminal: an undispatched queued request was withdrawn,
or a frozen native batch observed an authoritative cancelled terminal.
A consumed batch member may therefore transition from ``DEQUEUED`` to
``CANCELLED``; its original transcript and any partial shared answer remain.
A false daemon cancel acknowledgement alone never establishes this status.
Distinct from ``FAILED`` — cancellation is a deliberate non-error dismissal.

UploadedFile-Input.title: UploadedFile
UploadedFile-Input.description:
A reference to a file uploaded to a provider's file storage by ID.

This allows referencing files that have been uploaded via provider-specific file APIs
rather than providing the file content directly.

Supported by:

- [`AnthropicModel`][pydantic_ai.models.anthropic.AnthropicModel]
- [`OpenAIChatModel`][pydantic_ai.models.openai.OpenAIChatModel]
- [`OpenAIResponsesModel`][pydantic_ai.models.openai.OpenAIResponsesModel]
- [`BedrockConverseModel`][pydantic_ai.models.bedrock.BedrockConverseModel]
- [`GoogleModel`][pydantic_ai.models.google.GoogleModel] (Gemini API: [Files API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/files) URIs, Google Cloud: GCS `gs://` URIs)
- [`XaiModel`][pydantic_ai.models.xai.XaiModel]

media_type.title: Media Type
media_type.description:
Return the media type of the file, inferred from `file_id` if not explicitly provided.

Note: Inference relies on the file extension in `file_id`.
For opaque file IDs (e.g., `'file-abc123'`), the media type will default to `'application/octet-stream'`.
Inference relies on Python's `mimetypes` module, whose results may vary across platforms.

Required by some providers (e.g., Bedrock) for certain file types.

identifier.title: Identifier
identifier.description:
The identifier of the file, such as a unique ID.

This identifier can be provided to the model in a message to allow it to refer to this file in a tool call argument,
and the tool can look up the file in question by iterating over the message history and finding the matching `UploadedFile`.

This identifier is only automatically passed to the model when the `UploadedFile` is returned by a tool.
If you're passing the `UploadedFile` as a user message, it's up to you to include a separate text part with the identifier,
e.g. "This is file <identifier>:" preceding the `UploadedFile`.

``request_id`` identifies which secret of the request group this value is for

the user tweak the bot-suggested entry metadata before it is written. Omitted
fields fall back to what the bot originally requested. ``value`` is a

Send the secret exactly as stored — the pre-existing behaviour.

This is what every row created before schemes existed does, and it stays
the default, so the rows whose vault value already embeds ``Bearer `` keep
working untouched. It is also the deliberate escape hatch for any vendor
whose credential format we do not model, which is the same shape Postman
settled on: a closed set of composed types, plus one verbatim path.

WorkforceTaskLinkDirection.title: WorkforceTaskLinkDirection
WorkforceTaskLinkDirection.description:
A task link as seen from one task's perspective.

Not stored: computed when projecting a task's links. ``OUTGOING`` means the

WorkforceTaskLinkType.title: WorkforceTaskLinkType
WorkforceTaskLinkType.description:
Canonical type of a directed link between two workforce tasks.

Stored on ``workforce_task_links.link_type``. ``RELATES_TO`` is symmetric
(order-independent — a pair is stored once, in a canonical task-id order);
``BLOCKS`` is directional — the ``from`` task blocks the ``to`` task.

The reverse "blocked by" relationship is a *derived view* of a ``BLOCKS``
row seen from the ``to`` task's side (see ``WorkforceTaskLinkDirection``),
never a stored value — one relationship is always exactly one row.

AssistantAbortedEvent.description:
The in-flight assistant turn was aborted by a /stop (or one of the
other abort triggers — bare ``stop``, ``abort``, ``cancel``, etc.).

Non-terminal — a follow-up ``assistant.error`` (or ``assistant.end``)
closes the turn out for real. The dedicated event exists so clients
can distinguish "stopped on purpose" from "network failure / timeout"
and render a "Stopped" badge instead of an error toast.

``request_id`` identifies the message being aborted (NOT the /stop
message that triggered the abort). The /stop message is its own
chat.request with its own request_id.

Lets a client verify a realtime frame belongs to the channel it subscribed for and drop cross-channel misdeliveries. Optional so the field can roll out ahead of every publisher and consumer without a lockstep deploy; real publishers always set it.
conversation_id.title: Conversation Id

aborted_by.description: Actor id (sender_id) that issued the /stop, when known.
aborted_by.title: Aborted By

AssistantCancelledEvent.description:
A still-queued request was cancelled by the user before it ever ran.

never dispatched, so there is no visible assistant response of its own). The
dedicated event lets connected clients drop the message from the queued tray

truth is the persisted ``turn_status='cancelled'``.

``request_id`` identifies the cancelled queued message.

AssistantEndEvent.description:
Bot finished streaming (chat.done).

``message_id`` and ``ordinal`` identify the cold-started answer row (claimed
at ``chat.picked_up``, before any content). Carrying both here lets a client
place the just-completed answer at its real consumed-order position
immediately — without waiting on the follow-up ``message.new`` or a refetch
to settle the synthetic streaming bubble (which, for runtimes whose terminal
frame has no id, never binds by id). Both are null only if the row was never
persisted (cold-start failed and no content arrived).

persisted.description: True when this terminal error is written to ``conversation_messages.errors`` as a durable in-chat error card. Set for a bot ``chat.error`` frame, which the persist loop always records, and for a genuine mid-turn bot disconnect, which always records one too — a ``generic`` card for an ordinary drop, a ``maintenance_restart`` card when the drop is a maintenance evict. A client may render the card live and suppress the generic error banner ONLY when this is true, because a matching persisted card is guaranteed to back it on refetch/reload. Terminals that intentionally persist no card — proxy idle timeout, a rollout drain (the partial is left adoptable instead), and the queued-turn reaper — leave this false, so clients keep their banner and never suppress it without durable evidence (see the web chat's isTurnFailureShownInChat).

Present only alongside ``persisted=True``. Lets the client render the exact card live — the amber rate-limit card from a provider-error handoff, or the neutral maintenance-restart card — instead of a generic one it would otherwise have to swap out on refetch. Null when the persisted card is generic or for non-persisted terminals.

ConversationTurnEvent.description:
A conversation's active turn started or ended.

Published to the conversation's *sidebar* channel — ``org:{org_id}`` for
org-scoped conversations, the owner's ``personal:{user_id}`` for user-scoped
ones — exactly like :class:`ConversationActivityEvent`. Lets aggregate
surfaces (workforce boards, sidebars, launchpad) drive their "bot is working"
pulses from the one or two shared channels every client already holds,
instead of live-subscribing to one ``conversation:`` channel per watched
conversation (Centrifugo caps a connection at 128 channels; EPIC #3530).

The event mirrors the ``conversation_active_turn`` lease, which is what the
bulk ``/active-turns`` poll reads: ``started`` is published when a turn
claims the lease, ``ended`` only when that turn's terminal actually released
it. It is a compact lifecycle edge, never a stream — deltas stay on the
conversation channel. Best-effort: a missed ``ended`` (crashed publisher,
dropped socket) is repaired by the active-turn poll.

``request_id`` names the turn that produced the edge. Two turns' edges can
reach a client out of order (a successor's ``started`` can overtake its
predecessor's ``ended``), so a consumer applies an ``ended`` only when it
names the turn it currently believes is running.

conversation_id.description: Conversation whose turn changed state
conversation_id.title: Conversation Id

request_id.description: Turn that produced this edge. Apply an ``ended`` only if it names the turn last seen ``started``; a stale one from a superseded turn is ignored.
request_id.title: Request Id

state.description: ``started`` when a turn claimed the conversation's active-turn lease; ``ended`` when the owning turn's terminal released it.

ConversationTurnEvent.title: ConversationTurnEvent

ConversationTurnState.description: Edge of a conversation's active-turn lease, announced as ``conversation.turn``.
ConversationTurnState.title: ConversationTurnState

ContentBlockPayloadRef.description:
Reference to the conversation-scoped file holding a block's heavy data.

The bytes live in conversation-scoped storage owned end-to-end by
``ContentBlockService`` and are served at read time by the content-block
serving endpoint, exactly like conversation attachments — so access is
gated by access to the conversation. The block persists an opaque, durable
``payload_id`` (never a storage key or presigned URL): the service *derives*
the storage location from the caller's already-authorized
``(org, conversation, payload_id)`` context, so clients never see — and can
never supply — a raw object key. The message read path's re-signers only
refresh user-prompt parts and the ``media`` column, not tool-return
metadata, so an ID that is resolved server-side on every read is also what
keeps references from going stale.

payload_id.description: Opaque durable ID of the payload document (a UUID). Hand it back to the content-block serving endpoint / read tool together with the conversation to fetch the rows — storage location is server-internal.
payload_id.title: Payload Id

conversation_id.description: Conversation the payload file is scoped to; gates read access.
conversation_id.title: Conversation Id

content_type.description: MIME type of the payload file (``application/json`` for chart/table data).
content_type.title: Content Type

byte_size.description: Payload size in bytes — lets the frontend show a size hint / guard huge fetches.
byte_size.title: Byte Size

ContentBlockPayloadRef.title: ContentBlockPayloadRef

ContentBlockResult.description:
What the block-emitting tools (``emit_content_block``, ``send_files``) return.

``block`` is the slim reference the frontend renders (carried on the tool
return's structured output). ``summary`` is the only part the model reads
back — a one-line description so the agent can refer to what it emitted
without re-ingesting the payload.

block.description: The content block the frontend renders.
block.title: Block

summary.description: One-line summary for the model (the only part it re-reads).
summary.title: Summary

ContentBlockResult.title: ContentBlockResult

CreditsExhaustedContentBlock.description:
The org ran out of Botyard-managed LLM credits mid-tool, as a top-up card.

A tool that spends the org's managed credits (``generate_image``) returns this
instead of failing, so the chat shows the same "Out of AI credits" card it
shows when a chat turn exhausts them, call to action included. It is a
*result* rather than an error because a failed tool return has no structured
channel to the renderer on any runtime: only a successful return's
structured output reaches ``packages/chat``.

The block deliberately carries **no link**. Where to top up is host routing
state (the console mounts a billing context; the embeddable widget, whose
readers are the org's customers, never does), so the renderer, not the tool,
decides whether a call to action appears. Always managed credits: a BYOK
exhaustion is the customer's own provider account, which a Botyard top-up
cannot clear, and no BYOK path emits this block.

message.description: Server-composed, user-facing explanation. Never provider text, never a link or a settings path.
message.title: Message

CreditsExhaustedContentBlock.title: CreditsExhaustedContentBlock

DiagramContentBlock.description:
A rendered diagram (Mermaid). The diagram source lives in the payload file.

The inline block carries only tiny frame metadata (title/description/height);
the potentially-large Mermaid source text is the heavy payload, stored in the
referenced file exactly like a chart's rows — so the diagram source never
crosses the chat/LLM boundary. The frontend fetches the source by
``payload_id`` and renders it with Mermaid (lazy-loaded, console-side); the
widget/embed bundle, which excludes the heavy renderer, falls back to showing
the source text.

``height`` is an optional max render height in px; the emit tool clamps a
supplied value into ``[DIAGRAM_HEIGHT_MIN_PX, DIAGRAM_HEIGHT_MAX_PX]`` so a
stored block can't request an absurd card size. ``None`` means auto-size.

title.description: Optional title shown above the diagram.
title.title: Title

description.description: Optional subtitle/description.
description.title: Description

height.description: Optional max render height in px (auto-size when omitted). Clamped by the emit tool to a sane bounded range.
height.title: Height

payload.description: Conversation file holding the Mermaid source text.

DiagramContentBlock.title: DiagramContentBlock

FileBlockEntry.description:
One file attached to a :class:`FilesContentBlock`.

Like :class:`ContentBlockPayloadRef`, this is a **reference**: the bytes live
in conversation-scoped storage and the block persists only an opaque, durable
``file_id``. A presigned URL is deliberately *not* stored — the message read
path re-signs user-prompt parts and the ``media`` column but **not** tool-return
metadata, so a URL frozen into a block would expire and leave a permanently
dead card. The serving endpoint mints a fresh URL from the caller's already
authorized ``(org, conversation, file_id)`` context on every read instead.

The inline ``filename`` / ``content_type`` / ``byte_size`` are the *display*
copies: they let the card draw a labelled chip immediately, before (or without)
fetching a download URL. The serving endpoint returns the authoritative values
read back from storage.

file_id.description: Opaque durable ID of the stored file (a UUID). Hand it back to the content-block file endpoint together with the conversation to get a fresh download URL — storage location is server-internal.
file_id.title: File Id

filename.description: Display name of the file, e.g. ``q3-report.pdf``.
filename.title: Filename

content_type.description: MIME type, used to pick the chip icon / inline preview.
content_type.title: Content Type

byte_size.description: File size in bytes — rendered as a size hint on the chip.
byte_size.title: Byte Size

caption.description: Optional per-file caption shown beneath the file's chip or thumbnail.
caption.title: Caption

checksum.description: Optional SHA-256 hex digest of the file's bytes, computed while streaming it out of the sending bot's workspace. Lets a recipient verify the download matches what was sent.
checksum.title: Checksum

FileBlockEntry.title: FileBlockEntry

FilesContentBlock.description:
One or more files a bot sent into the conversation, rendered as a card.

Unlike chart/table/diagram — one block, one payload document — a files block
holds a *list* of independent file references, so it carries per-file refs
inline rather than a single ``payload``. Nothing about the bytes is parsed
server-side, so any file type is accepted; the renderer decides from
``content_type`` whether a given entry previews inline (images) or shows as a
download chip.

title.description: Optional title shown above the files.
title.title: Title

description.description: Optional subtitle/description for the group as a whole.
description.title: Description

files.description: The files in this block, in the order the bot sent them.
files.title: Files

FilesContentBlock.title: FilesContentBlock

McpConnectFormKind.description:
Which install a ``FORM`` connect card submits, as the human.

* ``VENDOR_CREDENTIALS`` — a credential tile: the vendor's own fields,
  submitted to the credential install (``POST .../connections/credentials``).
  Secret fields there take vault *entry ids*.
* ``TEMPLATE`` — a template tile with a configuration form, submitted to the
  ordinary MCP server create. Secret fields there take vault *key paths*.
